ChronoVisor

ChronoVisor (Paper version)

The cluster's control-plane and coordination authority. One of ChronoLog's three top-level components — alongside the ChronoKeeper (tail operations) and the tiered ChronoStore (ChronoGrapher writes, ChronoPlayer reads). It sits off the data path (events never flow through it) and instead manages client connections, chronicle metadata, and time.

“The ChronoVisor handles client connections and chronicle metadata information. It also acts as the global clock enforcing time synchronization between all server nodes participating in a ChronoLog cluster.”

At a glance

RoleControl plane / coordination authority; off the data path
DeploymentSingle dedicated node, typically the cluster head node
TimeMaster global clock; cluster nodes sync to it, clients derive relative ChronoTicks from its (base, rate)
MetadataOwns the chronicle namespace, tags, properties, permissions, and acquisition / reference counts
BootstrapInitializes ChronoKeeper structures, spawns the ChronoGrapher, configures KVS ranges, inits the ChronoPlayer
ConnectionsClient registry; entry point for connect / disconnect
MigrationInter-cluster ChronoVisor synchronization for moving chronicles
API surfaceAdmin API (registry + clock) and Chronicle API (metadata)

Responsibilities

Connections & registry Entry point of the cluster. Clients must register before any operation; the ChronoVisor's URL (chronolog://<host>:<port>) is what connect() targets, and disconnect() tears the connection down.
Global clock Runs the master clock. Server nodes sync to it at init and periodically. Clients keep their own clocks and instead receive (base, rate) via sync_clock() to compute correct ChronoTicks — the time-based event IDs.
Chronicle metadata Owns the namespace (create / edit / destroy) and the acquisition lifecycle (acquire / release). Maintains the reference counter that guides tiering and gates deletion (reference_count == 0), plus tags: type, granularity, tiering policy, permissions, coherency, and collision semantics.
Bootstrap & init Orchestrates the rest of the cluster: initializes ChronoKeeper structures (tail hashmap and backlog at init; data hashmaps and chronicle index on create/acquire), spawns the ChronoGrapher and configures its KVS key ranges, inits the ChronoPlayer, and passes chronicle tags to the ChronoKeeper to enforce collision policy.
Migration Coordinates moves ChronoVisor-to-ChronoVisor. Because ChronoTicks are offsets from a base value, the destination computes its distance and drift from the source so client tick calculations still resolve to the correct slot.

Why it's designed this way

ChronoLog's goal is to avoid a centralized sequencer or metadata lock for finding the log tail — the bottleneck in Corfu (sequencer) and Bookkeeper (MDM locking). The ChronoVisor is deliberately kept off the per-event hot path: it never assigns log positions and never sees event data. Ordering comes from physical time via ChronoTicks, leaving the ChronoVisor only the lighter, less-frequent work — shared time and metadata — so record/playback stay lock-free. This is why the paper lists ChronoLog's tail location as “MDM lookup (lock-free)”.

Note: reflects the architecture described in the ChronoLog research paper; the current codebase may have evolved the ChronoVisor's responsibilities since.

ChronoVisor (Implementation)

As built on develop, the ChronoVisor is a single-process C++ server (chronovisor_instance) that runs two Thallium/Margo RPC services and holds metadata in memory. It is still the cluster's coordinator and entry point, but its scope is narrower than the paper: a connection + metadata + service-registry hub. It is off the data path, and — notably — it has no clock role.

Source: src/chrono-visor/ — chronovisor_instance.cpp instantiates a VisorClientPortal and a KeeperRegistry, then idles until SIGTERM.

At a glance

ProcessOne server binary; no global clock thread. Holds metadata in-process.
ServicesVisorClientPortalService (client-facing) and VisorKeeperRegistryService (data-process-facing)
Data modelChronicle (namespace) → Story (acquirable, recordable unit) → Events. IDs are CityHash64(name).
Metadata storePlain in-memory unordered_maps under global mutexes (ChronicleMetaDirectory, ClientRegistryManager). Not distributed, not lock-free, not persisted.
TimeNone. Events are timestamped client-side (the client's high_resolution_clock); a Keeper-side clocksource class exists but is unused dead code.
Client APIConnect, Disconnect, CreateChronicle, DestroyChronicle, AcquireStory, ReleaseStory, DestroyStory, ShowChronicles, ShowStories

Responsibilities

Connections & registry Connect checks the client protocol version and registers the ClientId; Disconnect auto-releases any stories the client still holds (notifying their recording groups) before removing the record. Client records live in ClientRegistryManager.
Chronicle / Story metadata Create/destroy chronicle, destroy story, and acquire/release story — reference-counted via per-story acquisition counts and acquirer maps. Plus ShowChronicles / ShowStories. create_chronicle takes only a name: no tags, indexing granularity, or tiering policy.
Data-process orchestration heavy Via KeeperRegistry: Keepers, Graphers, and Players self-register (IdCards + periodic stats), and are organized into RecordingGroups (N keepers + 1 grapher + 1 player). On the first AcquireStory the Visor randomly picks an active RecordingGroup, records the binding, and notifies that group's Grapher, Keepers, and Player to start recording; on last release it notifies them to stop.
Routing the client AcquireStory returns the set of Keeper ServiceIds (where to record) and the Player ServiceId (where to replay). Record / playback / replay then go directly to those processes — never through the Visor.
Destruction lifecycle Destroying a chronicle/story broadcasts the destroy to all Graphers so persisted HDF5 files are cleaned up; metadata is removed first to close acquire/destroy races.

Not present (vs. the paper)

Global clock absentNo clock sync, no drift modeling, no ChronoTicks. A clock_offset parameter exists in ClientConnect but is dead — never set, never returned to the client.
Authorization stubAll authorization predicates return true (tracked in issue #637).
Durability / migration absentMetadata is in-memory only (lost on restart). No chronicle migration and no replication at the Visor.
Tags / policies absentNo indexing granularity, tiering policy, coherency, or collision-semantic tags; edit() does not exist.

Verified against src/chrono-visor/ on develop (chronovisor_instance.cpp, VisorClientPortal.cpp, ClientPortalService.h, ChronicleMetaDirectory.cpp, ClientRegistryManager.cpp, KeeperRegistry.h/.cpp, ChronoVisorConfiguration.cpp) and the Keeper clocksource in KeeperDataStore.cpp.

Gaps

The implementation keeps the paper's core principle — the ChronoVisor is a coordinator that stays off the data path — but it dropped/deferred the physical-time machinery that was the paper's headline contribution, added a real service-discovery layer the paper hand-waved, and reframed the user data model. The main differences:

AspectPaper versionImplementation (develop)
Global clock ChronoVisor is the master clock; clients fetch (base, rate) via sync_clock() and compute ChronoTicks; all servers sync to it. removed No clock at the Visor. Keepers timestamp locally with steady_clock; ordering is per-story at the recording Keeper, with time-chunking and an acceptance window. The dead clock_offset marks where it was meant to be.
Data model Chronicle = collection of stories, where a story is the sorted HDD-tier file; Event = (ChronoTick, value). reframed Chronicle = named namespace; Story = the user-facing acquirable log clients record to. The "sorted file" notion is now a Grapher HDF5 output, not the user abstraction.
Process orchestration Implied: the ChronoVisor "spawns" Keeper/Grapher/Player; discovery and binding largely unspecified. new scope A substantial KeeperRegistry: processes self-register, are grouped into RecordingGroups, and stories are load-balanced across groups with explicit start/stop notification and delayed-exit handling.
Client API surface connect/disconnect/sync_clock and the chronicle metadata ops create/edit/destroy/acquire/release. changed No sync_clock and no edit; added DestroyStory, ShowChronicles, ShowStories.
Metadata robustness Implied durable (and potentially distributed) metadata, plus migration and replication. prototype Single-node in-memory maps under coarse mutexes; no persistence, migration, or replication; authorization stubbed (#637).
Chronicle policies Visor owns per-chronicle tags: tiering policy, coherency, and collision semantics (A–D). absent No such tags at the Visor. An acceptance window exists at the Keeper; tiering is the Grapher's fixed pipeline.

Why they differ

Hard research problem The synchronization-free global clock via physical time was the paper's central thesis and its hardest piece. The current system sidesteps it: order events per-story at the Keeper rather than assign cluster-global ChronoTicks. The clock_offset stub shows the seam where it was planned.
Real deployments need plumbing A running cluster needs dynamic membership, fault handling, and read/write component coordination — so the KeeperRegistry/RecordingGroup layer is net-new scope the paper abstracted away as "the Visor initializes the components."
Usability of the abstraction Promoting Story to a first-class, acquirable client handle gives a clean acquire→record→replay lifecycle, at the cost of overloading the paper's "story" term.
Prototype maturity Persistence, migration, replication, authorization, and the rich tag/policy set are deferred features, not design reversals — some are tracked (e.g. auth in #637).

Net effect: the implementation is faithful to "Visor = off-path coordinator" but is not yet the physical-time log store the paper describes — it is a metadata + service coordination layer, with time-based ordering pushed down to the Keepers and several headline features still outstanding.

Differences

A simpler, hand-maintained list of the key paper-vs-implementation differences for the ChronoVisor. Each entry recaps what the paper proposed and how the implementation diverges, so it stands on its own without re-reading the full sections above.

  1. Global clock & time synchronization. In the paper the ChronoVisor is the cluster's master clock — it hosts the global time source, synchronizes all participating server nodes, and hands each client a (base, rate) pair to derive drift-corrected ChronoTicks; this was its headline responsibility. The implementation Visor has no clock role at all — it neither hosts a clock nor synchronizes nodes, so that entire duty is removed from the component (only a dead clock_offset parameter marks where it was meant to live).
    Core idea is system-wide, not Visor-exclusive

    Although the clock lived on the Visor, the decision to order events without a synchronized global clock (local timestamps + composite event identity) is a system-wide conceptual approach, not a Visor-only choice — it is analyzed in Data Model → Differences: “Physical time & ChronoTick”. Whether to revive a global clock is a general-architecture question that spans the whole system, so it belongs to that broader discussion rather than being settled here.

  2. Process orchestration & service registry. The paper leaves this largely unspecified — the Visor “spawns” the Keeper, Grapher, and Player, with discovery and binding hand-waved. The implementation builds a dedicated subsystem (KeeperRegistry): the data processes register themselves with the Visor (IdCards plus periodic stats that double as liveness) and are organized into RecordingGroups — N Keepers with one Grapher and one Player. On the first AcquireStory the Visor binds the story to an active group and notifies it to start recording; on the last release it notifies it to stop, so recording follows the same reference count that gates the metadata. The client is handed the group's Keeper and Player service IDs and talks to them directly, while delayed-exit handling and the periodic stats provide basic membership and fault tracking.
    Why we made this difference

    A running cluster needs dynamic membership, fault handling, and read/write coordination that the paper abstracted away as “the Visor initializes the components.” Self-registration was chosen over the paper's spawn model because it fits the HPC / Mochi execution model — the job scheduler launches the processes and they announce themselves — and it decouples coordination from process lifecycle, so the Visor reflects membership rather than supervising processes. The net effect is that the Visor traded the clock role for an orchestration role the paper never specified: its center of gravity moved from “global time + metadata” to “metadata + cluster-recording coordinator.”

  3. Metadata durability. The paper treats the Visor as the cluster's authoritative, durable metadata store. In the implementation the chronicle namespace (ChronicleMetaDirectory) and the client registry (ClientRegistryManager) are in-memory only — plain unordered_maps with no persistence. A Visor restart or crash loses the entire namespace (every chronicle, story, acquisition, and client record), while the Graphers' HDF5 files survive on disk — leaving orphaned data the Visor can no longer address. The bytes persist; the metadata that gives them meaning does not.
  4. Availability & replication. The paper implies a fault-tolerant metadata authority; the implementation runs a single Visor with no replica. It is therefore a single point of failure for the whole control plane — while it is down, no client can connect, create, or acquire (in-flight writes to already-acquired stories continue, since they bypass the Visor, but no new work can start). There is no metadata replication.
  5. Distribution & migration. The paper gestures at distributed metadata and inter-cluster chronicle migration (moving chronicles between ChronoVisors). The implementation holds the whole namespace in one process's heap: it is not partitioned across nodes, so the namespace is bounded by a single node's RAM, and there is no migration mechanism at all.
  6. Coarse-grained metadata locking. Each metadata store sits behind one global mutex (g_chronicleMetaDirectoryMutex_, g_clientRegistryMutex_), so every metadata operation — create, destroy, acquire, release, show — serializes against all the others. The paper's lock-free ethos applies to the data path; the control-plane metadata is the opposite — a coarse whole-directory lock. It is a scaling ceiling rather than a hot-path concern, since metadata operations are far less frequent than events.
  7. Authorization. The paper assumes the Visor enforces access control — permissions on chronicles and stories. The implementation scaffolds but does not implement it: every operation (connect, create, destroy, acquire, release) calls an authorization predicate and returns CL_ERR_NOT_AUTHORIZED on failure, but all three predicates — is_client_authenticated, chronicle_action_is_authorized, and story_action_is_authorized — return true unconditionally (tracked in #637). The gate is wired but inert.
  8. Client API surface. The client-facing API the Visor exposes is not identical to the paper's — methods are renamed and re-shaped (e.g. create(name, index, tags) → CreateChronicle(name), acquire → AcquireStory(chronicle, story)), and story-level operations are added (DestroyStory, ShowChronicles, ShowStories). Conceptually the structure is unchanged: connect plus chronicle / story metadata management.
    Core idea belongs to the data model

    The API only changed shape because the data-model approach changed underneath it (Story as a first-class acquirable unit, no chronicle tags). It is the surface, not the decision — the reasoning lives in the Data Model and API tabs.

  9. Chronicle policies & tags. In the paper the Visor owns a rich per-chronicle tag set — type, indexing granularity, tiering policy, coherency, collision semantics, and permissions. The implementation Visor handles none of them: create_chronicle takes only a name, and the tag / policy structures are inert or absent.
    Core idea belongs to the data model

    Tags and policies are a data-model concept, not a Visor mechanism — their absence is analyzed in Data Model → Differences: “Tags, types & policies”. The Visor simply has nothing to store because the model upstream does not define them.

Areas of Research, Analysis & Improvement

1 · Rename the Keeper registry Improvement

KeeperRegistry (and the VisorKeeperRegistryService) also register Graphers and Players and own the RecordingGroups, so the Keeper prefix is misleadingly narrow. Rename the subsystem to something scope-accurate — e.g. RecordingRegistry. Low-risk but multi-file: the class, the RPC service, headers, and config / log strings.

2 · Deployment & orchestration layer Analysis

Today the cluster is brought up by an external parallel-ssh bash script (tools/deploy/deploy_cluster.sh) and the components self-register, so the Visor has no runtime control or scaling. Add a deployment layer — but as an operational tool, not a runtime component (a persistent peer would create a who-launches-the-launcher problem and fight the HPC batch model).

How. Harden the script and delegate process placement to the platform — Slurm / mpirun on HPC, a Kubernetes operator or Helm chart on cloud — with the tool owning config generation, RPC-conf validation, and start / stop / health; a step further is a job-scoped controller that the scheduler launches first to bring up and monitor the rest within the allocation and expose a scale / restart / status API. Why. This recovers the paper's one-touch control-and-scale intent without re-coupling remote spawning back into the Visor, and leans on battle-tested schedulers instead of reinventing process management.

3 · Metadata durability Improvement

How. Persist the Visor's metadata so it survives restart — a write-ahead log plus periodic snapshot, or back the namespace and client registry with an embedded durable KV (e.g. RocksDB). Why. Today a restart loses the whole namespace and orphans the on-disk HDF5; persistence makes the metadata recoverable and re-bindable to the data already on disk. (Difference 3.)

4 · Availability & replication Analysis

How. Replicate the Visor for failover — a Raft-replicated metadata state machine, or externalize metadata to a proven coordination service (etcd / ZooKeeper) providing replication and quorum. Why. Removes the single point of failure so the control plane survives a Visor crash; externalizing can deliver durability and replication in one step. (Difference 4.)

5 · Distribution & migration Analysis

How. Partition the namespace across multiple Visors (shard by chronicle / hash) so it is not bounded by one node's RAM, and add the paper's inter-cluster chronicle migration (export / import of a chronicle's metadata, with clock reconciliation). Why. Lets the namespace scale out and supports moving chronicles between clusters, as the paper envisioned. (Difference 5.)

6 · Finer-grained metadata locking Analysis

How. Replace the single global mutex per store with finer-grained locking — per-chronicle / per-story locks, sharded maps, or lock-free reads — so independent metadata operations stop serializing. Why. The current whole-directory lock is a scaling ceiling under high client / chronicle concurrency; finer locking lifts it without touching the data path. (Difference 6.)

7 · Authorization Improvement

How. Implement the stubbed authorization framework — establish client identity from the connect-time euid / credentials (rather than trusting it), define a permission model for chronicles and stories (owner / ACL / capabilities), and make the three predicates actually enforce it. Why. The gate is already wired into every operation but unconditionally returns true (#637); without real enforcement there is no access control or multi-tenant isolation — a production prerequisite. (Difference 7.)

Data Model

Data Model (Paper version)

A three-level hierarchy Chronicle → Story → Event, ordered by physical time. The defining idea: an event's identity is its time — a single ChronoTick serves as both its position and its key, so no sequencer is needed to order the log.

Entities

Chronicle A named, user-created log: a series of events ordered by physical time. Assigned a base value (creation timestamp from the global clock) at creation, and indexed at a configurable granularity (ns default; coarser units group events). Carries a tags structure (size, ownership, permissions, access mode) and properties: type (e.g. prioritized), indexing granularity, auto-tiering policy, coherency semantic.
Story The storage form of a chronicle's events: on the HDD tier, events are sorted then written sequentially to a file — the "story". A chronicle is a collection of stories; a story is a collection of ordered events. (On upper tiers events instead live as KV pairs in the journal / KVS.)
Event A key–value pair: key = ChronoTick, value = an uninterpreted byte array. The smallest unit of addressing.
ChronoTick A monotonically increasing uint32_t = time distance from the chronicle's base value, at the chronicle's granularity. Computed client-side from the ChronoVisor's (base, rate) and the client's own drift. It is the event's position/ID — there is no separate sequencer.

Ordering, collisions & mutability

OrderingGiven directly by ChronoTick (physical time).
CollisionsAt coarse granularity several events may share a tick. Four configurable semantics, set in chronicle tags at creation: A link all in arrival order; B keep last; C keep first, reject the rest; D first keeps the slot, others spill to the next slots.
MutabilityAppend-only and immutable: no in-place update; only range deletes at the very beginning or end. Backdated events outside the acceptance window are rejected.
Operationsrecord (append), playback (tail read), replay (range / catch-up read with an optional constraint).

Note: reflects the data model as described in the ChronoLog paper.

Data Model (Implementation)

The implementation keeps the names Chronicle → Story → Event but redefines them. An event's identity is a composite tuple (eventTime, clientId, eventIndex) — not a single time tick — and the persisted form is a time-windowed HDF5 chunk, not a sorted PFS file.

Source: client/cpp/include/chronolog_types.h, chronolog_client.h, src/chrono-common/include/StoryChunk.h, StoryChunkWriter.{h,cpp}, src/chrono-visor/include/Chronicle.h & Story.h, client StorytellerClient.cpp.

Core types

ChronicleA namespace. ChronicleId = uint64 = CityHash64(name). A Visor-side metadata record holding a map of Stories.
StoryThe acquirable, recordable unit. StoryId = uint64 = CityHash64(chronicleName + storyName) (so story names are unique per chronicle).
LogEventThe real event: { storyId, eventTime (u64), clientId (u64), eventIndex (u32), logRecord (string) }. Used over RPC and in storage. The client-facing Event is the same minus storyId (the story is implied by the handle).
EventSequencetuple<eventTime, clientId, eventIndex> — the key that uniquely orders an event within its story.
StoryChunkAll events of one story over [startTime, endTime), held as an ordered map<EventSequence, LogEvent>. The unit of data movement and of storage.

Ordering & timestamping

eventTimeThe client's local high_resolution_clock epoch-nanoseconds, read at log time. Uncorrected — no base value, drift, or offset is applied; the Visor is not consulted.
eventIndexA per-client monotonic atomic counter.
OrderLexicographic on (eventTime, clientId, eventIndex). The (clientId, eventIndex) tail deterministically breaks ties — so there are no configurable collision semantics; collisions are impossible by construction.
Append pathThe client picks a Keeper (round-robin) and sends the LogEvent directly to it. Ordering originates entirely client-side.

Physical storage

FormOne HDF5 file per StoryChunk: <chronicle>.<story>.<startTimeSeconds>.vlen.h5, a compound dataset of {storyId u64, eventTime u64, clientId u32, eventIndex u32, logRecord vlen-bytes}. Written by the Grapher. A CSV extractor also exists.
Not presentNo sorted-sequential PFS file via MPI-IO, and no separate SSD key-value journal tier — the path is Keeper memory → Grapher → chunk file.

Scaffolding present but not wired inert

Attrs / tagsChronicleAttrs / StoryAttrs (indexing granularity {ns,us,ms,sec}, default ms; type {standard, priority}; access permission), metadataMap_ / propertyList_, and an Archive map exist on the Visor classes but are inert: create takes only a name, there is no edit, and granularity is never used for indexing.
Legacy EventA separate Event class (sid, timestamp, void* data) in the Visor is unused by the live path.

Verified against the files listed above on develop, plus the Keeper clocksource in KeeperDataStore.cpp.

Gaps

Same root cause as the ChronoVisor: the physical-time / ChronoTick machinery was the paper's hard contribution and is deferred. Event identity moved from "time alone" to "time + client + index", which is sequencer-free and collision-free without needing a synchronized clock — at the cost of the paper's single-integer addressing and its tiering model.

AspectPaper versionImplementation (develop)
Event identity One ChronoTick (uint32): time-distance from the chronicle base value. Key is the time. reframed Composite EventSequence (eventTime u64, clientId, eventIndex); the byte payload is a separate field.
Time source Drift-corrected relative time computed from the ChronoVisor's global clock (base, rate). removed Raw client high_resolution_clock nanoseconds, uncorrected; the Visor is never consulted.
Base value & granularity Per-chronicle base value; configurable indexing granularity groups events onto ticks. absent No base value; absolute ns timestamps; the granularity enum exists but is inert (default ms, unused).
Collisions Four configurable semantics (A–D) set in chronicle tags. structural None needed — (clientId, eventIndex) breaks every tie deterministically.
"Story" The sorted HDD file is the storage form. reframed A user-facing acquirable handle; the storage form is the time-windowed StoryChunk (HDF5 file).
Storage / tiering NVMe journal → SSD KVS → sorted HDD story (multi-tier). simplified Keeper memory → Grapher → one HDF5 chunk file per window (single persisted form; CSV optional).
Tags / type / policy Rich chronicle tags own tiering policy, coherency, and type (e.g. prioritized). inert The structs exist on the classes but are not wired to the API.
Mutability Append-only + range-delete at the ends; acceptance window rejects backdated events. partial Append-only; an acceptance window exists at the Keeper; range-delete / re-index are not exposed.

Why they differ

Deferred research core The global-clock / ChronoTick scheme was the headline contribution and the hardest to get right, so it was deferred — identity shifted to a composite key that needs no synchronized clock.
Collisions designed out Because (clientId, eventIndex) makes two events' keys distinct by construction, the A–D collision machinery became unnecessary — trading the paper's single-integer addressing for guaranteed uniqueness.
Simpler persistence Self-describing HDF5 chunk files replaced the sorted-PFS story plus KVS journal: one persisted form, easier to write and read, but not the multi-tier pipeline the paper benchmarks.
Stubbed, then left The attrs / tags / archive scaffolding shows the paper model was partially typed into the classes and then left unwired — consistent with granularity, tiering policy, and prioritized chronicles being deferred features.

Net effect: the stored data is faithfully per-story, time-ordered events, but ordering is built from uncorrected client clocks + a composite key rather than the paper's drift-modeled ChronoTicks — and the multi-tier, tag-driven chronicle is not yet realized.

Differences

A simpler, hand-maintained list of the key paper-vs-implementation differences for the data model — each one with the reason it exists.

  1. Physical time & ChronoTick. The paper orders events with a clock-synchronized ChronoTick. No clock synchronization has been implemented, so time is taken in a simpler way — each client's own local clock, uncorrected. The ordering logic and structure are kept (events are still ordered by time); only the clock-sync part is left undeveloped.
  2. Uniqueness & collisions. Because that (local) time is not precise enough to be a unique identifier on its own, standard uniqueness practice was used instead: the single ChronoTick index is replaced by an EventSequence that adds clientId and eventIndex. This guarantees uniqueness by changing the method — designing collisions out (unique by construction) rather than the paper's detect-and-resolve (collision detection + semantics).
  3. Base value & granularity. The paper makes each ChronoTick relative to the chronicle's base value (its creation time), at a configurable granularity (ns / µs / ms / sec). Relative ticks give a shared time reference across unsynchronized clients, can be remapped on migration, and fit in a compact uint32. The implementation uses absolute uint64 nanosecond timestamps instead — no base, and no granularity grouping (the enum exists but is inert) — which is simpler and avoids wraparound, at the cost of those three benefits.
    Why #3 is benign — the reasoning behind it

    Difference #3 describes the change neutrally; this is why the absolute choice loses nothing important. The relative scheme's three motivations mostly dissolve for a single-cluster deployment:

    Shared frame. A Visor-adjusted timestamp already places every client in a common reference frame; subtracting the chronicle base is a uniform shift applied identically by all clients, so it adds nothing to agreement — it only buys a smaller number. Migration. Reconciling two clusters needs the same information either way — the origin clock's offset/drift to the destination — which relative does not get for free (the destination still measures it). Within a shared reference, absolute needs no recompute at all; and the real-world solution for geo-distributed ordering (Google Spanner's TrueTime) uses globally-synchronized absolute time, not per-object bases. Compactness. The only surviving edge is the uint32 key — but the pipeline is I/O-bound, so the saving is marginal, and the small integer actively forces a range ↔ resolution tradeoff and more tick collisions (coarse granularity packs more events onto one tick), making the uniqueness problem worse.

    Net: absolute uint64 matches or beats relative on shared frame, migration, range/resolution, and collision pressure, conceding only a marginal compact key. The implementation's choice is not a regression — it is arguably the stronger engineering decision, so we can build on it without concern.

  4. Story — a new level of abstraction. The model gains a level by shifting roles up by one and adding a new top. The Event is unchanged; the paper's Story (the internal sorted storage file) becomes the StoryChunk; the paper's Chronicle (the user-acquired recording unit) becomes the Story (now a named, acquirable unit); and a new top-level Chronicle is added as a pure namespace. So the hierarchy goes from Chronicle → Story(file) → Event to Chronicle(namespace) → Story(handle) → StoryChunk → Event.
    Why #4 enriches the model — and what it enables

    Unlike #1–#3, this difference is additive, not subtractive. It adds one user-facing level (Story) while leaving event semantics untouched — the same immutable, time-ordered events. The payoff is organizational: many independent streams can live under one Chronicle namespace and be recorded and replayed independently, which means more ways to organize data and therefore more application patterns. The only direct cost is a few extra story-level APIs (AcquireStory / ReleaseStory / ShowStories). The organizational richness is essentially free.

    The new level also enables finer-grained optimization: with Story as a first-class, addressable unit, the system can bind, own, distribute, and tune work per story — opening the door to better load distribution and performance — all while the underlying logic stays the same. The abstraction opens those options; it does not, by itself, impose them.

    To evaluate later — Keeper / Grapher architecture

    The optimization options the Story level opens are realized by additional, separable processing decisions: the StoryChunk granularity, the StoryPipeline (the ordered, distributed timeline of a story's chunks), and RecordingGroups (binding a story to a fixed set of keepers + exactly one grapher for clean consolidation). These are opt-in machinery, not required by the data model: a minimal binding (acquire → one keeper + one player) is intrinsic, but the full group / pipeline elaboration could be dropped and the Story data model would still stand — you would simply forgo the per-story distributed ingestion and load distribution.

    Whether this machinery is the right approach — and how it is designed — belongs to the Keeper and Grapher tabs, where it is evaluated. It is parked here only because it is the reason-and-consequence of this data-model change.

    To evaluate later — the event → chunk flow shift

    #4 also moved the inter-component data flow from event-based to chunk-based. Ingest stays per-event (client → Keeper, one LogEvent per RPC), but everything from the Keeper onward (Keeper → Grapher → disk) moves per StoryChunk — batched and presorted; the Keeper is the transition point. Ironically, the paper marketed per-event distribution and real-time per-event flushing as advantages — the implementation traded both for batching.

    Benefit: throughput — amortized per-RPC / network overhead, sequential + presorted I/O, fewer coordination ops. Tradeoffs: higher durability latency (an event is not flushed until its chunk closes ≈ chunk duration + acceptance window); a larger crash-loss window (un-flushed events sit in volatile Keeper memory; no replication); more Keeper memory held; and coarser distribution (cohesive per-story chunks instead of the paper's any-keeper per-event spread). The chunk time-window is the knob that dials throughput vs. latency / durability. To be evaluated in the Keeper / Grapher tabs.

  5. Tags, types & policies. The paper attaches a rich, configurable tag bundle to each chronicle — set at creation and editable — that drives behaviour: type (e.g. prioritized), auto-tiering policy, coherency semantic, permissions / access mode, ownership, and size. (Indexing granularity and collision semantics, also paper tags, are covered in #3 and #2.) This per-object configurability is a capability still to be developed — and, because the model now has two levels (#4), it must be reframed across both Chronicle and Story: deciding which attributes belong at the chronicle (namespace) level, which at the story (stream) level, and how they compose.
    Why #5 matters — and which parts are actually worth it

    The concept is valuable, but not uniformly — each tag is worth weighing on its own before building any of it:

    Permissions / ownership. High value — table-stakes for any shared, multi-user system (though it partly overlaps the surrounding HPC access controls). Auto-tiering policy. Valuable only once a real multi-tier storage hierarchy exists — gated on that bigger piece. Type / prioritized. Useful under multi-tenant contention (QoS); premature without contention to arbitrate. Coherency as a per-object knob. Likely over-engineering — a single good default usually suffices. Size. A cheap stat, useful mainly as an input to quotas or tiering.

    The two-level hierarchy adds a design dimension: not just which tags, but at what level (chronicle vs. story) and how they compose / inherit. So the value is real but selective — it needs a deliberate decision on what to add and where.

  6. Mutability. The append-only core is identical — no in-place updates — and both whole-object delete and the acceptance window (rejecting backdated events) are shared. The paper additionally allows two controlled boundary mutations that are not exposed: range-trim (deleting the oldest or newest events, only at the ends, never mid-log) and re-index (changing granularity via edit). So the gap is narrow — just those two boundary operations.
    Where #6 is worth it — and how chunks help

    Head-trim (retention). The one genuinely useful piece — dropping data older than X to reclaim space is a standard need. And it is largely achievable without a new API: because StoryChunks are time-bounded HDF5 files, retention mostly reduces to deleting old chunk files. Restricting trims to the ends (never the middle) is exactly what keeps this tractable. Tail-trim (rollback). Undo a bad recent batch — niche, medium value. Re-index. Moot — it only matters with granularity bucketing, which the absolute-uint64 model (#3) deliberately doesn't use. Skip. Acceptance window. Necessary for a distributed time-ordered log, and already shared by both. No action.

    Net: the only substantive item is head-trim retention — mostly an Improvement, and partly a Grapher concern, since it owns the chunk files. The rest is either shared, niche, or moot.

Areas of Research, Analysis & Improvement

1 · Physical-time ordering & clock synchronization Research

ChronoLog began as a thesis about ordering by physical time: a global clock on the ChronoVisor, drift-modeled ChronoTicks as each event's identity, and total order achieved without a sequencer or locking. To ship a functional product, the implementation set that aside and gave each event a self-contained composite identity (eventTime, clientId, eventIndex) — which guarantees uniqueness structurally and needs no clock coordination at all. The headline research idea was deferred, not disproven.

The pragmatic consequence is striking: the system today never depends on clock quality, so the original thesis has never actually been tested in practice. But that same working system is now the ideal test bed and infrastructure to do that research for real. The pipeline is functional end to end (client → keeper → grapher → player), it is already keyed on time at every stage, and the clock machinery was deferred at two well-defined seams — both of which still carry the original stubs.

Where to intervene(1) the ChronoVisor publishes a clock reference at connect (the dead clock_offset is the stub); (2) the client's single timestamp function computes a corrected tick instead of a raw local clock (the ChronologTimer / chrono_tick names are the stubs).
Why it's a strong test bedThe existing composite key already produces a correct, unique ordering — a ground-truth baseline. Clock-derived ordering can be measured against it, so the research question sharpens from "can we order at all?" to "how close to true global time-order can we get, and with what uncertainty?"
Research arcMVP: offset-only client↔Visor sync, swap the timestamp source, measure ordering fidelity. Then: drift-rate modeling, Spanner-style uncertainty intervals, backdated-event handling, multi-client evaluation. Parity: server-to-server sync and collision semantics, as needed.

In short: the deviation that made ChronoLog usable also turned it into the right vehicle for the physical-time research it was born from — a functional substrate with a measurable baseline, waiting at two seams the authors already shaped.

2 · Event uniqueness: “design-out” vs. “detect-and-resolve” Research

The two versions answer the same problem — physical time is not unique (many events can land on one tick) — in opposite ways. The paper detects and resolves collisions: events with the same tick are routed to one server, detected, and reconciled by a configurable per-chronicle policy (semantics A–D) plus an acceptance window. The implementation designs them out: the composite key (eventTime, clientId, eventIndex) makes two events' keys distinct by construction, so no detection, routing constraint, or policy is needed. The research question: with a working clock in place, which strategy actually wins — on throughput, tail latency, storage overhead, and ordering fidelity?

Why it's only fair under Thread 1Without synchronized clocks, "tick collisions" are mostly clock skew, not true concurrency. A meaningful comparison needs the clock work above first; Thread 1 enables this study.
The honest novelty barNeither idea is new on its own — composite (time, node, seq) keys are standard (Hybrid Logical Clocks, Cassandra, Kafka), and the paper already published the physical-time approach. A reviewer's first question is "what's new vs. HLC and the original paper?" The contribution must be empirical or a new mechanism, not the keys themselves.
Where a real contribution could live(a) A rigorous head-to-head at HPC scale on a real tiered store — using the composite key's exact order as a ground-truth oracle for clock-derived order (an unusual, clean methodology). (b) A new mechanism the test bed enables: online clock calibration from the oracle, cheap bounded-uncertainty ordering, or adaptive switching between strategies by observed contention.
Realistic venueA solid evaluation + artifact fits mid-tier systems / HPC venues (HPDC, CCGrid, Cluster, IPDPS, ATC). Top-tier (SOSP / OSDI / NSDI) needs the new mechanism or a surprising result — which has to come out of the research, not be promised up front.

Working hypothesis (to be measured, not assumed): design-out likely wins on throughput (the pipeline is I/O-bound, so key size barely matters) and on simplicity (zero coordination), while detect-and-resolve buys configurable semantics and provenance trade-offs. Before committing the team, scope it with a tight lit scan vs. HLC, TrueTime, and recent shared-log work (Scalog, Boki, FlowLog) to lock down the “what's new.”

3 · Configurable tags, types & policies Analysis Improvement

Conceptually interesting and potentially high-benefit: richer organization, QoS (priority), security (permissions / ownership), and capacity control. But the benefit is selective and the design is non-trivial — especially now that the model has two levels — so it splits into analysis and improvement.

AnalysisDecide which tags and categories are actually worth adding (authz is high value; tiering policy is gated on a real multi-tier hierarchy; priority is premature without contention; configurable coherency is likely unnecessary; size is a trivial stat), and — given Chronicle + Story — at which level each belongs and how they compose / inherit.
ImprovementThen build the worthwhile ones. Permissions / ownership (authz) is the clearest near-term candidate; the rest follow their gating conditions.

Because the model now has two abstraction levels, this is no longer a single chronicle-level tag set: it must be reframed across both Chronicle and Story — what is namespace-wide vs. per-stream, and how attributes inherit.

4 · Boundary mutation & retention Analysis Improvement

From Difference #6: the append-only core is fine, but the paper's controlled boundary mutations are not exposed. Only one is worth pursuing — retention via head-trim — and there is a cheap path to it, so the work is to decide exactly what makes sense and how.

AnalysisDecide whether a dedicated range-trim / retention API is worth building, or whether deleting old chunk files (the Grapher already owns them) covers the need. Weigh tail-trim (rollback) as a niche extra; skip re-index (moot without granularity bucketing).
ImprovementImplement retention (head-trim) — most likely via chunk-file deletion coordinated with the Grapher — with trims restricted to the ends to stay tractable.

The acceptance window already handles backdated events, so it needs nothing here. Retention is partly a Grapher concern (chunk-file lifecycle), so the design crosses the data-model / storage boundary.

API

API (Paper version)

A client-library API in three groups — Admin, Chronicle, and Event. Operations address data through opaque handles: acquire returns a Chronicle ID (CID), and record returns an Event ID (EID). Time management is explicit through sync_clock.

Admin API

connect(URL) → statusConnect to the cluster via the ChronoVisor's URL.
disconnect() → statusTerminate the connection.
sync_clock(URL) → base, rateFetch the ChronoVisor's global clock value and drift rate. Called on connect, periodically, and on chronicle creation / migration.

Chronicle API

create(name, index, tags) → statusCreate a chronicle with an indexing granularity and an attribute set (type, permissions, tiering policy, …).
edit(name, index, tags) → statusRename, re-index, or re-tag a chronicle.
destroy(name, flags) → statusDelete a chronicle once all acquisitions are released.
acquire(name, flags) → CIDAcquire (optionally exclusive / partial) and get the Chronicle ID.
release(CID, flags) → statusRelease an acquisition (drops the reference count).

Event API

record(CID, data) → EIDAppend serialized data; returns the Event ID.
playback(CID) → dataTail read: get the data at the end of the chronicle.
replay(CID, range, constraint) → dataCatch-up read of a range (a vector of <startEID, endEID>), optionally filtered by a constraint.

Note: reflects the API as described in the ChronoLog paper (Fig. 2).

API (Implementation)

A C++ chronolog::Client facade. The shape is close to the paper, but addressing is by name strings (not opaque CID/EID), writing goes through an acquired StoryHandle, the only "event ID" is the event's own timestamp, and there is no tail-read — reads are time-range replays.

Source: client/cpp/include/chronolog_client.h; StorytellerClient.cpp (write), ChronologClient.cpp / ClientQueryService.cpp / PlaybackQueryRpcClient.cpp (read).

Session

Client(portalConf)
Client(portalConf, queryConf)		Construct writer-only (portal only) or writer + reader (with a query service). Reads require the second form.
Connect() → intRegister with the ChronoVisor; exchanges a wire protocol version (currently 2).
Disconnect() → intDisconnect; auto-releases any still-held stories.
client_id() → ClientIdThis client's packed id (ip / port / pid), as it appears on every event it produces.

Chronicle & Story

CreateChronicle(name) → intCreate a chronicle — name only, no index or tags.
DestroyChronicle(name) → intDestroy a chronicle.
AcquireStory(chronicle, story) → {int, StoryHandle*}Acquire a story by name; returns a write handle bound to the story's Keepers.
ReleaseStory(chronicle, story) → intRelease a story.
DestroyStory(chronicle, story) → intDestroy a story.
ShowChronicles() → {int, [name]}List chronicles.
ShowStories(chronicle) → {int, [name]}List a chronicle's stories.

Event write

StoryHandle::log_event(record) → uint64Append a record. The client stamps eventTime / eventIndex, picks a Keeper (round-robin) and sends directly. Returns the eventTime (the de-facto event ID), or 0 on failure. There is no Client::record.

Event read

ReplayStory(chronicle, story, start, end, vector<Event>&) → intRead events in the time window [start, end) into a vector. Served by the Player (internally a "playback request").
ReplayStory(chronicle, story, start, end, EventCallback) → intStreaming overload: invoke a callback per event, no client-side vector materialization.

Verified against chronolog_client.h and the client write/read implementation on develop. No sync_clock, edit, or tail-read exist in the surface.

Gaps

The implementation's verbs are recognizably the paper's, but the differences fall into two distinct kinds that are worth keeping apart. Contract differences are operations the paper specified that the implementation changed or dropped — genuine paper-vs-implementation divergence. Realization choices are dimensions the paper left unspecified — it defines an operation set, not how the client is packaged — that a working client library still had to decide; these are additions, not reversals. Most of the contract differences track the same deferred features seen in the other tabs.

Contract differences paper specified · implementation changed

AspectPaper versionImplementation (develop)
Addressing Opaque handles: acquire → CID, record → EID; later ops take the id. reframed By (chronicle, story) name strings; the only handle is a StoryHandle for writing; the only id is the event's timestamp.
Clock API sync_clock() → (base, rate) for drift-corrected ChronoTicks. removed No clock call — clients stamp their own local time.
Create / acquire args create(name, index, tags), acquire(name, flags). absent CreateChronicle(name) / AcquireStory(chronicle, story) — no index, tags, or flags.
Edit edit(name, index, tags) (rename / re-index / re-tag). absent No edit operation.
Write record(CID, data) → EID on the client. reframed StoryHandle::log_event(data) → eventTime; sent directly to a Keeper, not via the Visor.
Tail read playback(CID) → data (the log tail). absent No dedicated tail-read; use a recent-window replay.
Range read replay(CID, range, constraint): a vector of EID ranges + a filter. changed ReplayStory(…, start, end): one [start, end) time window, no constraint.

Realization choices paper unspecified · implementation decided

AspectPaper versionImplementation (develop)
Client packaging Unspecified — the paper lists operations, not whether the client is stateless calls or a stateful object. decided A stateful Client object: the Visor address is constructor config, and it holds the connection lifecycle, the assigned clientId, and the write engine.
Reader / writer modes Unspecified — a single, undifferentiated client. decided Built writer-only (portalConf) or writer + reader (+ queryConf); reads require the second form.
Protocol handshake Unspecified. decided Connect() exchanges CLIENT_PROTOCOL_VERSION (2); the Visor rejects mismatches with CL_ERR_PROTOCOL_VERSION_MISMATCH.
Streaming reads Unspecified — replay returns data. decided A second ReplayStory overload delivers per-event via an EventCallback, with no client-side vector materialization.

Why they differ

No clock, no tags No sync_clock and the empty create/acquire args follow directly from the deferred global clock and the inert chronicle tags documented in the other tabs.
Handle & name model Name-based addressing keeps the API stateless and human-readable; the StoryHandle binds a writer to the exact Keeper set the Visor returned at acquire, so each log_event goes straight to a Keeper. The EID became the event's own timestamp because the data model already keys on it.
Tail-read folded in With time-keyed events and Player-side range queries, a tail read is just a replay over a recent window, so a separate playback op was never built.
Operational hardening Reader/writer modes, the protocol handshake, and the streaming-callback read are production concerns the research prototype didn't address — net-new surface rather than design reversals.

Net effect: the paper's verbs survive, but the contract narrowed (no clock, no tags, no edit, no tail-read, name-addressed) while the realization widened (a stateful client, modes, a handshake, streaming). Metadata power down, operational surface up — and only the first column is a true divergence from the paper.

Differences

A simpler, hand-maintained list of the key paper-vs-implementation API differences. Several are direct consequences of the data-model differences already analyzed — noted briefly here and cross-referenced rather than re-derived.

  1. No sync_clock. The paper's clock-sync Admin call is gone — the implementation orders events by each client's uncorrected local time, so there is no global clock to fetch. Consequence of Data Model → Differences: “Physical time & ChronoTick”.
  2. Empty create / acquire args. CreateChronicle(name) and AcquireStory(chronicle, story) drop the paper's index, tags, and flags — there are no chronicle tags or policies for them to carry. Consequence of Data Model → Differences: “Tags, types & policies” and “Base value & granularity”.
  3. No edit. With no tags or indexing to re-set, the paper's edit operation has nothing to act on and was never built. Consequence of Data Model → Differences: “Tags, types & policies” / “Mutability”.
  4. No tail-read (playback). The paper's playback(CID) → data — read the log tail — has no dedicated implementation. The only read is a time-windowed ReplayStory(start, end), so a tail is approximated by replaying a recent window rather than asking for “the latest”. This is the one genuinely API-level capability that is missing rather than reframed or inherited from another tab. (Minor footnote: ReplayStory also drops the paper's replay constraint/filter and its multi-range vector, reading a single [start, end) window.)

Areas of Research, Analysis & Improvement

1 · The API has no research agenda of its own Analysis

Conceptually, the implementation follows the API the paper described. Every difference we found is one of two things: a downstream consequence of an architectural decision taken at the data-model or system-component level (the deferred global clock, the absent chronicle tags/policies, name-based addressing, the EID becoming the event's timestamp), or a plain implementation consequence (the stateful Client, reader/writer modes, the protocol handshake, write routing straight to the Keepers). The one genuinely API-level gap — no dedicated tail-read — is a small missing operation, not a divergence in approach.

The practical implication: the API will need analysis and improvement, but almost entirely as a reflection of the rest of the project's. Reintroduce the global clock and the chronicle calls regain their clock semantics; add tags and policies and create/acquire regain their arguments; and so on — the API surface follows. There is no API-specific problem that varies significantly or warrants dedicated research on its own. API improvements should therefore be tracked against the Data Model and component (ChronoVisor / Keeper / Player) research, with the single standalone exception of restoring a dedicated tail-read operation.

ChronoKeeper

ChronoKeeper (Paper version)

The gateway for all tail operations (record and playback) and the manager of the top tier (NVMe / NVRAM). It acts as a lock-free, distributed cache of the latest events on top of the ChronoStore, built on HCL distributed data structures over RDMA/RoCE.

At a glance

RoleGateway for tail ops (record + playback); top-tier cache of latest events
TierNVMe / NVRAM (highest)
TechHCL distributed data structures over RDMA/RoCE; lock-free
DeploymentPer compute node (co-located with clients) or a dedicated subset (e.g. 1:64)

The four data structures

Distributed journalData hashmaps on every Keeper server; O(1) insert; lock-free.
Chronicle indexAn ordered set of eventIDs per hashmap; O(log n); used by the Player to maintain order.
Tail hashmapchronicleID → array of the latest eventIDs per server; lock-free tail location.
Event backlogCircular queue of (chronicleID, eventID) already copied to the ChronoStore; marks events safe to evict.

Operations

record()Client computes a ChronoTick, uniform-hashes it to a serverID, and one RPC inserts into journal + index + tail (atomic, lock-free).
playback()Read the tail hashmap → find the max ChronoTick → play() that server (random read from the hashmap).

Note: reflects the ChronoKeeper as described in the paper (§III.B).

ChronoKeeper (Implementation)

A standalone C++ thallium/Margo + Argobots process that ingests events and pushes time-bounded StoryChunks downstream to the Grapher. Crucially it is ingest-only — it serves no read or playback (reads are the Player's job). There is no HCL, no distributed hashmap, and none of the paper's four named structures.

Source: src/chrono-keeper/ — ChronoKeeperInstance.cpp instantiates a KeeperRecordingService, a DataStoreAdminService, and a KeeperDataStore, and registers with the Visor's KeeperRegistry.

At a glance

RoleEvent ingest + downstream extraction. No reads.
RPC exposedKeeperRecordingService (record_event) and DataStoreAdminService (start_story_recording, stop_story_recording, shutdown_data_collection, collection_service_available).
Registers asA Keeper in a RecordingGroup, with the Visor.
Unit heldIn-memory per-story StoryChunks (map<EventSequence, LogEvent>) in a KeeperStoryPipeline timeline. Mutex-guarded std containers — not lock-free, not distributed.

Ingest pipeline

Ingestrecord_event → IngestionQueue (per-story double-buffered deques; an orphan queue if the story isn't open) → KeeperDataStore collection threads merge events into a KeeperStoryPipeline → time-bounded StoryChunks in a timeline map.
EvictionA chunk "decays" when now ≥ chunk.endTime + acceptance_window; decayed chunks are pushed to the Grapher via RDMA (Keeper initiates receive_story_chunk). Configurable story_chunk_duration_secs (30), acceptance_window_secs (10).
TimestampsCome from the client (LogEvent.eventTime); the Keeper does not stamp events. A ClocksourceCPPStyle class exists but is dead code.

Not present (vs. the paper) absent

ReadsNo read / playback / tail RPC of any kind.
HCL structuresNo distributed journal, chronicle index, tail hashmap, or event backlog — by name or equivalent. The only RDMA use is point-to-point StoryChunk transfer to the Grapher.

Verified against ChronoKeeperInstance.cpp, KeeperRecordingService.h, DataStoreAdminService.h, KeeperDataStore.cpp, KeeperStoryPipeline.cpp, IngestionQueue.h on develop.

Gaps

The Keeper is the component that diverges most from the paper. The entire tail-read apparatus — tail hashmap, chronicle index, journal, backlog — is gone, because the implementation serves no tail-read at all: the Keeper is a pure ingest + forward stage, and reads come from the Player's archive.

AspectPaper versionImplementation (develop)
Reads / playbackGateway for tail reads via playback(). removed None — ingest-only; reads served by the Player from disk.
Tail locationLock-free tail hashmap (chronicleID → latest eventIDs per server). absent No tail concept; clients never query a tail.
Data structuresHCL distributed journal / index / backlog over RDMA. reframed Local mutex-guarded std deques/maps; RDMA used only to ship StoryChunks to the Grapher.
UnitPer-event insert into distributed hashmaps. reframed Per-story, time-bounded StoryChunk buffer.
Eviction triggerBacklog of events already copied to the store. changed Time-decay (endTime + acceptance_window).
Tier roleNVMe cache that serves the latest events to readers. reframed In-memory buffer that forwards chunks; serves nothing to readers.

Why they differ

No tail-read APIThe journal / index / tail-hashmap existed to make lock-free tail reads fast. With all reads served by the Player from archived chunks and no tail-read in the API, those structures had no consumer.
Simpler transportHCL distributed shared structures were replaced by a local buffer plus point-to-point RDMA chunk push — matching the StoryChunk-centric data model.
Narrowed roleThe Keeper became a pure ingest + forwarding stage, collapsing the paper's dual record + playback gateway down to record-only.

Net effect: a fast, simple write intake — but not the lock-free, latest-events tail cache the paper centers on.

Differences

A simpler, hand-maintained list of the key paper-vs-implementation differences for the ChronoKeeper. Each entry recaps what the paper proposed and how the implementation diverges, so it stands on its own without re-reading the full sections above.

  1. Keeper does not persist data — RAM only. In the paper the Keeper is the durable top tier — an NVMe / NVRAM cache that holds the latest events. The implementation's Keeper holds recent events in volatile RAM only (mutex-guarded per-story StoryChunks in a KeeperStoryPipeline) and persists nothing locally; durability is the Grapher's job.
    Why we made this difference

    Keep the Keeper a lean ingest path. Local persistence — storage I/O, fsync, journal management — would contend with the ingestion-critical section and cap throughput, so durability was moved entirely to the Grapher. The cost is that un-drained events live only in volatile RAM with no replication, so a Keeper crash loses them; that exposure is accepted because the Grapher owns durability and the chunk window bounds the loss window.

  2. Keeper does not serve tail reads — ingest-only. In the paper the Keeper serves both sides of the tail — record and playback (reading the most recent events directly from the Keeper). The implementation's Keeper is ingest-only: its sole client RPC is record_event, and it exposes no read or playback endpoint. Reading is entirely the Player's job (recent data from the Player's replica, older data from the persisted archive).
    Why we made this difference

    Serving reads from the Keeper would put bursty, unpredictable read load in contention with the steady write firehose — same RPC threads, same network, lock contention on the in-memory data. Keeping the Keeper a dedicated ingestion path protects its throughput ceiling, which — because ingestion is the system's input rate — is the whole system's ceiling. The resulting freshness gap is recovered off the hot path by the Player replica (below); why this corner was chosen is the subject of the tradeoff-triangle analysis in this tab.

  3. Keeper pushes data — rather than being pulled. In the paper the store copies events out of the Keeper (the event backlog tracks what has been copied to the ChronoStore and is therefore safe to evict) — a pull/copy driven by the downstream tier. The implementation inverts this: the Keeper proactively pushes each decayed chunk downstream, initiating the receive_story_chunk transfer to the Grapher over RDMA, and evicts on decay.
    Why we made this difference

    Pushing keeps the Keeper free of externally-driven traffic: it never serves pull requests reaching into its memory, and it controls its own drain timing — flushing a chunk exactly when it decays, which keeps memory bounded and predictable. It is the same principle as removing reads: nothing outside the ingest path gets to reach in and compete for the Keeper's resources.

  4. Eviction trigger. In the paper a chunk/event leaves the Keeper once it has been copied downstream — the event backlog tracks (chronicleID, eventID) pairs already copied to the ChronoStore and marks them safe to evict (copy-confirmed eviction). In the implementation eviction is time-driven: a StoryChunk “decays” when now ≥ chunk.endTime + acceptance_window_secs (default 10s on a 30s chunk), and the decayed chunk is then drained to the Grapher. The trigger to finalize a chunk is the clock, not a downstream copy-confirmation.
    Why we made this difference

    The acceptance window does double duty — it is the grace period the Keeper waits for late / out-of-order (backdated) events before closing a chunk, and the eviction trigger. A time-based close fits the chunk-based, clock-free model: a chunk is finalized when its window has elapsed, not when each event is individually confirmed persisted. It also decouples the Keeper from downstream acks — no per-event backlog bookkeeping, no waiting on the Grapher — keeping the ingest path simple. The trade is that finalization is driven by a timer rather than the paper's copy-confirmed safety, so durability rests on the push succeeding (compounding the volatile-RAM caveat from the no-persist difference).

  5. Keeper works in chunks — not single events. The paper records and moves data as single events (per-event record, per-event distribution and flushing). The implementation ingests per-event but, from the Keeper onward, moves data as time-bounded StoryChunks — batched and presorted. The Keeper is the event → chunk transition point.
    Why we made this difference

    Batching amortizes per-RPC, per-network, and per-I/O overhead and lets every downstream stage do sequential, presorted I/O — a large throughput win. The cost is durability latency (an event is not flushed until its chunk closes) and coarser distribution granularity than the paper's per-event spread. The full tradeoff and the tuning knob are analyzed in Research → “Event → chunk data-flow shift”.

  6. Dual extraction — the Player gets the latest. The paper served recent reads from the Keeper itself. The implementation instead extracts each decayed chunk to two consumers — the Grapher (persist) and the Player (which thereby holds the latest data in RAM) — so the Player can serve recent reads and merge them with the persisted archive. This is net-new (no paper analog) and currently staged: the Player receives and stores the chunks and PlaybackService is structured to merge an in-memory-recent tier with the archive, but the in-memory serving path is not yet fully wired.
    Why we made this difference

    It delivers low-latency recent reads without re-burdening the Keeper: rather than serve reads from the Keeper, the latest data is replicated to the Player — off the hot path — where read load scales independently and the Keeper's ingestion ceiling stays intact. The cost is a constant second extraction of every chunk, paid whether or not anyone reads; the chunk window tunes how fresh the replica is versus how much that extraction costs. See the tradeoff-triangle analysis for why this corner was chosen.

  7. Data structures: distributed → local. In the paper the Keeper's state lives in four HCL distributed structures spanning all Keeper servers over RDMA — a distributed journal (where events land), a chronicle index (ordering), a tail hashmap (lock-free tail location), and an event backlog (eviction). The implementation holds state in local, single-node std containers: per-story std::deque buffers in an IngestionQueue and an std::map timeline of StoryChunks in a KeeperStoryPipeline. Nothing spans Keepers; RDMA is used only to ship chunks downstream. The tail hashmap — and with it any queryable notion of “the tail” — is gone.
    Core idea is system-wide, not Visor- or Keeper-exclusive

    The distributed, tick-keyed design existed because the paper's record() hashes a ChronoTick across servers — the structures are the embodiment of the physical-time, sequencer-free scheme. With no global clock (and a per-story, recording-group-bound chunk model), there is no tick to distribute by and no reason to span Keepers, so the structures collapse to local per-story buffers. The driving decision is the system-wide clock / data-model one — see Data Model → “Physical time & ChronoTick” and the clock difference — not a standalone Keeper choice.

  8. Ingestion: lock-free → mutex-guarded. The paper's HCL structures are lock-free — record() inserts with no mutex on the hot path, a headline of its design. The implementation serializes ingestion with mutexes: a std::shared_mutex over the IngestionQueue's per-story handle map and an std::mutex (ingestionMutex) in the KeeperStoryPipeline. Ingestion is mutex-guarded, not lock-free.
    Why we made this difference

    Once the structures became local and single-node, plain mutex-guarded std containers were the simple, correct choice to ship — lock-free programming is hard to justify without the distributed-research substrate. The cost is real, not cosmetic: mutex contention under high ingestion concurrency can cap throughput, and because the Keeper's ingestion ceiling is the system's ceiling, that directly limits the whole system. Restoring lock-free or finer-grained ingestion is a candidate improvement (see Research).

  9. Event ordering & timestamping. In the paper the Keeper is where order is assigned: the client computes a clock-synchronized ChronoTick and the Keeper orders by it (with a chronicle index maintaining that order). In the implementation the Keeper stamps and orders nothing — events carry a client-assigned timestamp (LogEvent.eventTime) and order is implicit in the EventSequence key of the sorted StoryChunk. A ClocksourceCPPStyle class exists in KeeperDataStore.cpp but is dead code; the Keeper uses raw now() only for chunk-decay timing, never to stamp or order events.
    Core idea is system-wide, not Keeper-exclusive

    The paper made the Keeper the point where physical-time order is assigned; that is the heart of the clock-synchronized ChronoTick scheme. With no global clock, ordering moved to client timestamps + composite identity, and the Keeper's clocksource became an unused stub — the Keeper-side seam of the same decision the Visor's dead clock_offset marks. The driving choice is the system-wide clock / data-model one (Data Model → “Physical time & ChronoTick”), not a standalone Keeper decision.

  10. Drain-outage recovery — stubbed. The paper's copy-confirmed eviction is inherently safe: a downstream stall merely delays eviction. The implementation evicts on a timer (see Eviction trigger) and pushes chunks downstream, but its recovery path for a downstream outage is unimplemented — flush_outage_buffers() in KeeperExtractionChain is an empty //TODO #635. If the Grapher / Player drain stalls or fails, there is no mechanism to buffer-and-replay the affected chunks, so — combined with time-decay eviction and volatile RAM — a drain outage can silently lose data.

Areas of Research, Analysis & Improvement

1 · The Keeper tradeoff triangle Analysis

Nearly every Keeper difference flows from a single architectural decision. The Keeper's recent-data path balances three goals that cannot all be maximized at once — you can have about two, and must decide where to sacrifice the third:

  1. Ingestion throughput. The Keeper's ceiling — and because ingestion is the system's input rate, the whole system's ceiling. The thing most worth protecting.
  2. Tail-read latency. How quickly the freshest events become readable.
  3. Resource economy. No constant duplication of data or extra bandwidth / hardware.

The three viable designs each sit on one edge — gaining two, sacrificing one:

  1. Paper — Keeper persists & serves reads. Gains tail-read latency + economy (on-demand, no duplication); sacrifices ingestion — persist + read contend on the Keeper.
  2. Archive-only — no replica. Gains ingestion + economy; sacrifices tail-read latency — reads wait for persistence.
  3. Current — RAM-only Keeper + Player replica. Gains ingestion + tail-read latency; sacrifices economy — constant double extraction.

The implementation chose ingestion + tail-read latency, paying with economy (the constant second extraction to the Player), and made the sacrifice tunable via the chunk window (story_chunk_duration_secs / acceptance_window_secs) — shrink it for fresher reads, widen it to amortize the cost. It is the right corner for ChronoLog because the Keeper's ceiling is the system's ceiling, and the economy cost is bounded and isolable (downstream RDMA egress, off the ingest-critical section) rather than the unpredictable hot-path contention the other corner would impose.

To improve / decide: finish wiring the Player in-memory tier; make the window workload-adaptive and the chosen sacrifice explicit per deployment; and re-test the assumption with profiling — if the constant double extraction proves to eat into ingestion, the corner is worth revisiting. Every other Keeper difference (no reads, no local persistence, dual extraction) is a face of this one decision.

2 · Event → chunk data-flow shift Analysis

A consequence of Data-Model Difference #4: the implementation moved inter-component data flow from event-based to chunk-based. This is an engineering trade-off (throughput vs. latency / durability), not a research question — a tuning and prioritization decision to evaluate.

What changed: ingest stays per-event (client → Keeper, one LogEvent per RPC), but everything from the Keeper onward (Keeper → Grapher → disk) moves per StoryChunk, batched and presorted — the Keeper is the transition point. The benefit is throughput: amortized per-RPC / network overhead, sequential presorted I/O, and fewer coordination ops.

The cost is durability latency (an event is not flushed until its chunk closes ≈ chunk duration + acceptance window), a crash-loss window (un-flushed events sit in volatile Keeper memory, no replication), Keeper memory held until chunks decay, and coarser distribution (cohesive per-story chunks vs. the paper's any-keeper per-event spread). The knob is the chunk time-window, which dials throughput against latency / durability.

To analyze: whether the chosen window suits target workloads, and whether a hybrid (immediate per-event copy-down for durability + chunked bulk for throughput, as the paper's real-time flushing intended) is worth the added complexity.

The paper marketed per-event distribution granularity and real-time per-event flushing as advantages; the implementation traded both for batching. Mirrored from the Data Model tab (Difference #4), where the originating breadcrumb is kept.

3 · Lock-free / finer-grained ingestion Analysis

How. Replace the coarse mutexes on the ingest path — the IngestionQueue's std::shared_mutex and the KeeperStoryPipeline's ingestionMutex — with lock-free or finer-grained structures: per-story sharded locks, lock-free queues, or a single-writer-per-story design, so concurrent record_event calls stop serializing. Why. The Keeper's ingestion throughput is the whole system's ceiling, and mutex contention directly suppresses it; the paper's lock-free design targeted exactly this. (Difference: Ingestion — lock-free → mutex-guarded.)

4 · Drain-outage recovery Improvement

How. Implement flush_outage_buffers() (#635) — buffer chunks that fail to drain during a downstream (Grapher / Player) outage and replay them on recovery — and/or gate time-decay eviction on drain-confirmation (or a bounded retry) so a stalled drain cannot drop a chunk. Why. With time-decay eviction and volatile, unreplicated RAM, a drain outage currently risks silent data loss; the scaffolded outage buffer is the intended safety net but is inert. (Difference: Drain-outage recovery — stubbed.)

ChronoGrapher

ChronoGrapher (Paper version)

Continuously persists events from the Keeper journal down to the ChronoStore. A decoupled, elastic Apache Flink streaming job with a server-pull eviction model, structured as a three-node DAG.

At a glance

RolePersist events to the lower tiers (SSD KVS → HDD stories)
TechApache Flink streaming DAG
ModelDecoupled, elastic, server-pull eviction
DeploymentBurst-buffer / data-staging nodes

The three DAG nodes

Event CollectorPulls events from the Keeper journal, writes them to a distributed KVS (BigTable-style key ranges preserving temporal locality), and marks them safe in the backlog.
Story BuilderGroups eventIDs by chronicle; a story-creation epoch (by count, size, or timer) closes; a parallel sort runs; emits storyID + set<eventIDs> (no data movement).
Story WriterRange-gets from the KVS, buffers, and writes the whole story to HDD via MPI collective I/O as a ChronoLog-specific file.

Note: reflects the ChronoGrapher as described in the paper (§III.C).

ChronoGrapher (Implementation)

A standalone C++ thallium/Margo + Argobots process that receives whole StoryChunks pushed from the Keepers and writes one HDF5 file per chunk. No Flink, no KVS, no MPI collective I/O, no separate sort/builder stage.

Source: src/chrono-grapher/ — ChronoGrapher.cpp instantiates a GrapherRecordingService, a DataStoreAdminService, and a GrapherDataStore, and registers with the Visor as a Grapher.

At a glance

RolePersist StoryChunks to HDF5 (CSV optional).
IngestThe Keeper pushes serialized StoryChunks via RDMA into receive_story_chunk. Not a journal pull, not a KVS.
RPC exposedGrapherRecordingService (receive_story_chunk) and DataStoreAdminService (start/stop recording, destroy_story, destroy_chronicle).
UnitOne StoryChunk in → one HDF5 file out.

Pipeline & persistence

Pipelinereceive_story_chunk → ChunkIngestionQueue → per-story StoryPipeline (merges / re-chunks by time granularity) → extraction queue → HDF5FileChunkExtractor. Chunks become writable by time-decay, not by count/size.
File<chronicle>.<story>.<startSec>.vlen.h5: group /story_chunks, dataset data.vlen_bytes, compound {storyId u64, eventTime u64, clientId u32, eventIndex u32, logRecord vlen}.
Write modePlain serial HDF5 (H5Cpp, SWMR) with unique-filename rotation — no MPI-IO.
DestroyAsync: destroy_story / destroy_chronicle drain in-flight chunks, then delete matching HDF5 files.

Verified against ChronoGrapher.cpp, GrapherRecordingService.h, GrapherDataStore.cpp, HDF5FileChunkExtractor.cpp, and StoryChunkWriter.cpp on develop.

Gaps

Conceptually the Grapher still does the paper's job — move data from the fast tier to durable storage — but every piece of the paper's machinery (Flink, the KVS staging tier, the sort/epoch builder, MPI collective I/O) was replaced by a direct RDMA hand-off plus self-describing HDF5 files.

AspectPaper versionImplementation (develop)
RuntimeApache Flink streaming DAG. reframed Standalone C++ thallium / Argobots process.
IngestPulls events from the Keeper journal. changed Keeper pushes whole StoryChunks via RDMA.
Staging tierDistributed KVS with BigTable key ranges. absent None — chunks held in memory, then written.
Build stepGroup-by-chronicle + parallel sort + count/size/timer epoch. simplified Time-window merge; eligibility by time-decay only.
WriteWhole story via MPI collective I/O, bespoke file. changed One HDF5 file per chunk, serial writes (CSV optional).
Eviction modelServer-pull. mixed Keeper-push-triggered (the Grapher pulls the bytes via RDMA, but the Keeper initiates).

Why they differ

Heavy infra removedFlink + a distributed KVS + MPI-IO is a lot of moving infrastructure; a direct RDMA chunk hand-off into self-describing HDF5 files is far simpler to build and operate.
Chunk-native lifecycleWriting per-chunk (not per-whole-story) follows the StoryChunk data model and the time-decay lifecycle, removing the need for a separate sort/epoch builder and a KVS to stage from.
CostThe trade is the multi-tier KVS staging and collective-I/O throughput story the paper benchmarks — not realized here.

Net effect: a working, simple chunk → HDF5 file persister — without the KVS tier, parallel sort, or collective I/O the paper describes.

Differences

A simpler, hand-maintained list of the key paper-vs-implementation differences for the ChronoGrapher. Each entry recaps what the paper proposed and how the implementation diverges, so it stands on its own without re-reading the full sections above.

  1. Grapher receives pushed chunks — rather than pulling events. In the paper the Grapher's event collector pulls events from the Keeper journal (reading, not removing them), driving the data flow itself. In the implementation the Grapher is passive: it listens on receive_story_chunk and the Keepers push whole, pre-formed StoryChunks to it over RDMA. The Grapher no longer reaches into the Keeper or knows its journal — it waits to be handed chunks.
    Why we made this difference

    This is the Grapher's side of the Keeper's push decision (see ChronoKeeper → “Keeper pushes”): the Keeper controls its own drain timing and hands off finished chunks, so the Grapher needs no journal-pull machinery (collector processes matched to NVMe drives, knowledge of the journal layout). Just as important, the data arrives already grouped per-story and pre-sorted as chunks rather than as a raw, mixed event stream — which is the base that lets the later DAG work (the KVS staging tier, and the grouping and parallel sort) collapse, because the work they existed to do is already done upstream. (The build stage's merge survives — see Story building below.)
