  2. Data unit: events → StoryChunks. The paper's Grapher works in individual events — the event collector pulls events, writes them one-by-one into the KVS, and emits per-event (chronicleID, eventID) tuples. The implementation's transfer and processing unit is the whole StoryChunk: the Grapher receives, queues, and re-chunks per-story time-bounded chunks and never sees an individual event.
    Core idea belongs to the Keeper

    The Grapher is chunk-granular only because the Keeper produces and ships chunks — the unit was decided upstream, not here (see ChronoKeeper → “Keeper works in chunks, not single events”). It is a real Grapher-level fact — the whole pipeline is built around the chunk — but the decision and its rationale (batching for throughput) live with the Keeper and the data model.

  3. Event collection: the KVS staging tier is gone. In the paper the collection step writes pulled events into a distributed KVS — BigTable-style, one configurable time-range per SSD server — as an intermediate staging tier that preserves temporal locality and holds the mixed-chronicle event stream until the builder groups it. The implementation has no KVS and no staging tier: pushed chunks land in the Grapher's memory (ChunkIngestionQueue → per-story StoryPipeline) and are written straight to HDF5.
    Why we made this difference

    The KVS existed to stage and reorganize a mixed, unsorted event stream — preserve time locality and hold events across chronicles until they could be grouped and sorted. The chunk model does all of that upstream: a StoryChunk is already per-story, time-bounded, and sorted, so there is nothing for a staging / reorganization tier to do — the data is write-ready the moment it arrives. The cost is real, though: the KVS was also a durable SSD staging tier and a decoupling buffer, so without it recent chunks sit in volatile Grapher RAM until written (compounding the no-durable-staging theme), and the paper's three-tier hierarchy (NVMe → SSD-KVS → HDD) flattens to RAM → HDF5 files.

  4. Story building: group + sort → merge + re-window. In the paper the story-building step groups eventIDs by chronicle, closes a story on an epoch (count, size, or timer), and runs a parallel sort to produce an ordered story. In the implementation the grouping and sorting are gone — chunks arrive already per-story and internally sorted (by EventSequence) — but a real stage remains: the Grapher's StoryPipeline merges the chunk streams from the N Keepers recording the story into one ordered per-story timeline (storyTimelineMap) and re-windows them to its own granularity (Grapher chunk_granularity 60s, consolidating the Keeper's 30s chunks). Eligibility to write is by time-decay.
    Why we made this difference

    The grouping and the sort dissolved because the chunk model already does them upstream (a StoryChunk is per-story and internally ordered when it arrives), and the count/size/timer epoch collapses to the same time-decay used everywhere else. But the stage did not vanish: because a story is recorded by several Keepers in its recording group, their separate chunk streams must be interleaved into one coherent timeline, and re-windowing consolidates many small Keeper chunks into fewer, larger Grapher chunks (fewer output files). What changed in kind is that the paper's batch parallel sort — a compute-scalable DAG node — becomes an incremental merge of pre-sorted streams: cheaper, but no longer a scalable sort phase.

  5. Story writing: serial HDF5, not MPI collective I/O. In the paper the story writer uses MPI collective (parallel) I/O — many writer processes coordinating a single parallel write to a file on the HDD-based PFS. The implementation writes via plain serial HDF5 (H5Cpp, SWMR) with unique-filename rotation — one writer, no MPI, no collective I/O, no PFS dependency.
    Why we made this difference

    Collective I/O targets a parallel file system and coordinates many writers on one large file — a heavy dependency (an MPI runtime plus a PFS like OrangeFS). Writing self-describing HDF5 files independently is far simpler to deploy, and SWMR + unique filenames removes writer coordination entirely. But the cost runs deeper than bandwidth: parallel, multiple-writer (MWMR) I/O was a named contribution of the paper, which explicitly set out to beat the single-writer (SWMR) model of prior log stores. Serial HDF5 in SWMR mode lands back on exactly that SWMR model — so this is not merely “less optimized,” it forgoes one of the paper's headline contributions (and the ~3 GB/s with 32 collective writers it benchmarked). Note this is a usage limitation, not an HDF5 one — Parallel HDF5 over MPI-IO exists.

  6. Persistence unit: one file per chunk, not per story. In the paper the writer emits one file per whole story (the sorted story written out as a single ChronoLog file). The implementation writes one HDF5 file per StoryChunk (<chronicle>.<story>.<startSec>.vlen.h5), so a story becomes many small time-windowed files rather than one.
    Why we made this difference

    With chunks as the unit and no build stage to coalesce them, the natural output is one file per chunk — each file self-contained and written immediately on chunk decay, with no append or cross-chunk assembly. This is genuinely the Grapher's own call (it could buffer chunks into per-story files but chose not to). The cost is many small files per story instead of one: more files and metadata for the Player to open and merge on replay, and none of the single-file locality the paper's whole-story write provided.

  7. Storage destination: one local directory, not distributed auto-tiered storage. In the paper the Grapher writes into a distributed, multi-tier, auto-tiered store: data flows NVMe → SSD-KVS → HDD-PFS, the store spans burst-buffer / staging nodes and storage servers, capacity scales by auto-tiering across tiers (the paper's “3D log distribution”), and external connectors can push data out to a warehouse. The implementation writes every HDF5 file into a single configured local directory (HDF5FileChunkExtractor's rootDirectory, default /tmp) — one tier, one location, no auto-tiering, no connectors. The multi-tier distributed hierarchy collapses to flat files in a directory.
    Why we made this difference

    Auto-tiering across a distributed PFS is a large dependency (a tiered storage stack, OrangeFS, the KVS tier); flat HDF5 files in a directory are the minimal persister that runs anywhere — HPC, cloud, or a laptop. On the format, the choice is sound and arguably better than the paper's bespoke MPI-IO file: HDF5 is self-describing, standard, portable, and richly tooled, with SWMR built in — an HDF5 chunk is readable by anything, where the paper's file needs ChronoLog code. What is a stopgap is the serial, single-location usage, not HDF5 itself: HDF5 and parallelism are not exclusive (Parallel HDF5 runs over MPI-IO), so the evolution path is to keep HDF5 and layer parallel writes and tiering back on, not to replace it.

  8. Not elastic — a static process, not a grow/shrink DAG. The paper makes elasticity a named contribution: the Grapher's DAG nodes “grow or shrink based on the traffic,” adding collector / writer processes to match the I/O production and consumption rate. The implementation is a single standalone process with a static thread count (INGESTION_THREAD_COUNT, default 1) — no runtime grow/shrink, no per-traffic scaling; handling more load means redeploying with different config, not scaling dynamically.
    Why we made this difference

    Dynamic elasticity — spawning and retiring processing elements at runtime to track a fluctuating I/O rate — is significant machinery that Flink provided for free and that a hand-rolled C++ process does not. The implementation defers it: a static, configured process is simple and adequate for steady workloads. The cost is the paper's headline ability to match production and consumption rates under bursty load — under a spike the fixed Grapher becomes the bottleneck, with no way to absorb it by growing.

  9. Eviction without persistence confirmation. In the paper persistence is confirmed before eviction: after writing data down, the collector marks the Keeper's event backlog “safe to evict,” so the Keeper only drops what the Grapher has confirmed persisted — eviction is coupled to persistence success. The implementation has no such handshake: the Grapher sends no acknowledgment back, and the Keeper evicts each chunk on time-decay (see ChronoKeeper → “Eviction trigger”) regardless of whether the push landed or was persisted. If a push is lost — a network blip, a Grapher crash, a write error — the Keeper still deletes its only (volatile-RAM) copy on schedule, because it has no way to know.
    Why we made this difference

    It is the same decoupling that made the handoff simple: a Keeper that doesn't wait on per-chunk acks, and a Grapher that doesn't maintain a backlog, are each easier and faster. But the simplicity buys a silent-data-loss window — the confirmation loop the paper's backlog provided is gone, so nothing guarantees a chunk is durable before its source is dropped. This is not a consequence of push (a push could be acknowledged); it is the consequence of removing the acknowledgment.

  10. Outage-recovery is stubbed (#635) — on the Grapher too. The write side has a scaffolded-but-empty recovery path: GrapherExtractionChain::flush_outage_buffers() — meant to hold chunks that cannot be written during a write outage and replay them once it clears — is an empty //TODO #635. So a Grapher-side write outage (target unavailable, disk error, stalled extraction) has no replay: those chunks are lost. It is the same #635 gap found on the Keeper — the write-side half of the same handoff: with the confirmation loop gone (above), neither end has a safety net.

Areas of Research, Analysis & Improvement

1 · Durability vs. throughput Research

The one genuine open problem the Grapher's differences land on — the rest are deferred engineering. The implementation removed the paper's persistence-confirmation handshake: eviction is now decoupled from persistence success (see Differences — “Eviction without persistence confirmation” and “Outage-recovery is stubbed”), which opens a silent-data-loss window.

It is research, not a checkbox, because the naive fix — confirm-before-evict — reintroduces exactly the coupling the architecture removed for throughput: the Keeper's eviction (and therefore its memory pressure) would gate on the Grapher's persistence speed, so a slow Grapher stalls ingestion. So the open question is genuinely hard: how to guarantee a chunk is durable without coupling the ingest/write path to persistence speed. Candidate directions, each with real tradeoffs and none obviously right: replicate the Keeper's volatile buffer (memory / network cost), async acks with a bounded in-flight window (bounds loss rather than eliminating it), quorum / replicated persistence, or erasure-coding in-flight chunks.

This is the one conflict the paper itself leaves unsolved — durability vs. write latency — so our differences land on a real open problem, not an oversight to patch.

2 · Parallel writes (PHDF5) Analysis

How. Replace serial H5Cpp writes with Parallel HDF5 (PHDF5 over MPI-IO) so multiple writers persist concurrently. Why. Serial / SWMR writes forgo the paper's headline parallel-I/O (MWMR) contribution (~3 GB/s with 32 collective writers); PHDF5 keeps the self-describing format while restoring parallel bandwidth. (Difference: Story writing — serial HDF5, not MPI collective I/O.)

3 · Auto-tiering & distributed destination Analysis

How. Write to a distributed, multi-tier store rather than one local directory — restore SSD → HDD tiering (or modern equivalents) spread across storage nodes, plus the external connectors the paper described. Why. The implementation flattened the paper's hierarchy to flat files in /tmp; auto-tiering is what lets log capacity scale and keeps tail / historical I/O isolated. (Difference: Storage destination.)

4 · Elasticity Analysis

How. Make the Grapher's collector / writer parallelism dynamic — grow and shrink processing elements to track the I/O rate, instead of a static INGESTION_THREAD_COUNT. Why. Under bursty load a fixed Grapher becomes the bottleneck; elasticity (a paper contribution) is what matches production and consumption rates. (Difference: Not elastic.)

5 · Chunk coalescing Analysis

How. Coalesce multiple StoryChunks into fewer, larger files (toward the paper's one-file-per-story) instead of one HDF5 file per chunk. Why. One file per chunk yields many small files per story — more files and metadata for the Player to open and merge on replay; coalescing cuts that overhead. (Difference: Persistence unit.)

ChronoPlayer

ChronoPlayer (Paper version)

Serves historical reads (replay) from all tiers (Keeper + SSD + HDD). Deployed on all storage nodes, initialized by the ChronoVisor; a decoupled, elastic data-streaming job structured as a three-node DAG.

At a glance

RoleHistorical reads / replay
TiersAll: live Keeper events + SSD + HDD stories
ModelDecoupled, elastic streaming DAG; initialized by the Visor

The three DAG nodes

Replay HandlerPer-server request + response queues; the client randomly picks a server and pushes its replay request.
Range ResolverTurns a replay into a vector of ranges across tiers, splits it into ~4 MB subrequests, applies a constraint filter, and can short-circuit via the response queues.
Request ExecutorDedups ranges, aggregates over a replay epoch, fetches (range reads from SSD, parallel I/O from HDD), and contacts the Keeper if the end of the range is open.

Note: reflects the ChronoPlayer as described in the paper (§III.D).

ChronoPlayer (Implementation)

A standalone C++ thallium/Margo process that answers time-range replay queries by reading HDF5 chunk files from disk and RDMA-streaming a vector<Event> back. It reads only the disk archive — not the Keeper, not a live tier.

Source: src/chrono-player/ — ChronoPlayer.cpp instantiates a PlaybackService, a PlayerStoreAdminService, a live-chunk StoryChunkConsumerService, and an ArchiveReadingAgent (HDF5). The Visor assigns one Player per RecordingGroup.

At a glance

RoleRange replay from the HDF5 archive.
RPC exposedPlaybackService (story_playback_request(chronicle, story, start_time, end_time)) and PlayerStoreAdminService (start/stop recording notifications).
ReturnedA vector<Event> for [start, end), RDMA-bulk-transferred to the client.
Tiers readHDF5 files only.

Read path

Flowstory_playback_request → ArchiveReadingRequestQueue → ArchiveReadingAgent → HDF5ArchiveReadingAgent.
File locationThe agent keeps a (chronicle, story) → {startTime → filename} map (built by scanning story_files_dir, kept fresh by polling / inotify). For [start, end) it takes files from the last start ≤ start onward, reads each whole HDF5 file, filters events to the window, and stops once it passes end.
ResponseA cereal-serialized PlaybackQueryResponse is RDMA-bulk-pushed to the client's query service.

Stubbed / not present absent

Live-tier readDisabled: active_window_boundary is hardcoded to 1 and get_active_story_events is commented out — so no Keeper / top-tier read happens. (The Player does ingest live chunks into a PlayerDataStore, but the read path never queries it.)
DAG featuresNo range resolver, no ~4 MB subrequest split, no constraint filter, no range dedup / replay epoch, and no client random server selection (the Visor assigns one Player).

Verified against ChronoPlayer.cpp, PlaybackService.cpp, ArchiveReadingAgent.cpp, HDF5ArchiveReadingAgent.cpp, QueryResponseTransferAgent.cpp on develop.

Gaps

The Player delivers the paper's core promise — time-range replay — but as a single-tier, whole-file reader. The paper's defining feature, reading across all tiers (so a replay can reach right up to the live tail), is scaffolded but switched off.

AspectPaper versionImplementation (develop)
Tier coverageAll tiers (Keeper + SSD + HDD). stubbed HDF5 disk only; the live-window read is hardcoded off.
Server selectionClient randomly picks a storage server. changed The Visor assigns one Player per RecordingGroup.
Range resolverVector of ranges, ~4 MB subrequests, constraint filter. absent Whole-file reads; time-window filter only.
ExecutorRange dedup + replay epoch + parallel HDD/SSD reads. simplified One uniform HDF5 read per relevant file.
Open-ended rangeContact the Keeper for the latest events. absent No Keeper contact; archive only.
RuntimeStreaming DAG. reframed Poll queue → read files → one bulk transfer.

Why they differ

One persisted formWith a single HDF5 form on disk and the live-tier read not wired, the multi-tier resolver/executor machinery has nothing to resolve — a time-window scan of chunk files suffices.
RecordingGroup bindingOne-Player-per-group (Visor-assigned) replaced client random selection because the RecordingGroup model already binds a Player to each story.
Deferred optimizationsThe 4 MB split, dedup, replay epoch, and constraint filter are throughput / feature optimizations deferred in the prototype.
Half-built live readThe commented-out active-window branch and the unused PlayerDataStore show the all-tiers read was intended and partly wired, then left off.

Net effect: replay works over the persisted archive, but "read the whole log including the live tail in one call" — the paper's headline read feature — is not yet active.

Differences

A simpler, hand-maintained list of the key paper-vs-implementation differences for the ChronoPlayer. Each entry recaps what the paper proposed and how the implementation diverges, so it stands on its own without re-reading the full sections above. (As with the Grapher, the paper's use of Flink to build the read DAG is a prototype-realization choice, not a prescribed design, so it is not listed as a difference.)

  1. Reads only the archive — not all tiers (live read stubbed). In the paper the Player reads across all tiers — live Keeper events + SSD + HDD — so a single replay can span history and the live tail. The implementation reads only the HDF5 archive. It does ingest live chunks into a PlayerDataStore (the dual-extraction copy), but never queries it: the live-tier read is stubbed (active_window_boundary hardcoded to 1, get_active_story_events commented out).
    Why we made this difference

    Archive-only is the simplest functional read path, and the live tier is the in-progress half — the read side of the Grapher's dual extraction (see ChronoGrapher → “Dual extraction”). The machinery to serve recent data from the Player's RAM is staged but not wired, so today the freshest events are unreadable until the Grapher has persisted them — the same freshness gap as the Keeper tail, with the fix sitting half-built on the Player.

  2. Whole-file reads, not range reads. The paper fetches just the needed bytes — range reads from SSD, parallel I/O from HDD. The implementation reads each entire HDF5 file whose window overlaps [start, end) and filters events in memory, stopping once it passes end.
    Why we made this difference

    Whole-file reads are simple and fine while chunk files are small and self-contained. The cost is over-reading — the Player reads whole files to return a sub-window — which grows with file size and is the read-side counterpart of the Grapher writing one file per chunk.

  3. No constraint filter. The paper's replay can carry a constraint — a predicate that filters which events come back, beyond the [start, end) time window — and the Range Resolver pushes it down, refining the ranges so data that would be filtered out is never fetched (server-side filtering, less I/O). The implementation has no constraint: a replay returns every event in [start, end), and any filtering is left to the client to do after the full window has been transferred. This is the Player side of the API's dropped replay constraint.
  4. Query-optimizer stages dropped. The paper's read pipeline is not a plain fetch — its Range Resolver and Request Executor form a query optimizer over a multi-tier, multi-server read. The Range Resolver splits a large replay into ~4 MB subrequests (right-sized, parallelizable I/O units) and can short-circuit by peeking at the in-flight response queues — if a concurrent request already fetched that data, the read is skipped. The Request Executor then deduplicates overlapping ranges across concurrent replays (so the same chronicle region is never read twice) and aggregates requests over a “replay epoch” — a timer-closed batching window, configurable per chronicle, that groups many reads to minimize I/O while the timer prevents starvation. The implementation has none of these: each story_playback_request is handled on its own — locate the HDF5 files overlapping [start, end), read them, return. No subrequest split, no cross-request dedup, no epoch batching, no response-queue short-circuit.
    Consequence of the single-tier / single-Player simplification

    These optimizers exist to make concurrent, large, parallel reads efficient across many servers and tiers. With a single Player per group, whole-file reads, and one tier (see “Reads only the archive” above and the Grapher's storage-tier collapse), there are no cross-tier ranges to dedup, nothing to parallelize via subrequests, and no benefit to epoch-batching a single request stream. So the absence is a downstream consequence of the storage simplification, not a standalone read-design choice — restore parallel, multi-tier reads and these stages have to come back.

  5. Not elastic. Like the Grapher, the paper's Player is an elastic streaming DAG whose nodes grow and shrink with traffic; the implementation is a single static process. Same realization as ChronoGrapher → “Not elastic”.
  6. Client routing: one assigned Player, not a client-chosen server. In the paper the client randomly picks a Player server (per-server request / response queues). In the implementation the Visor assigns one Player per RecordingGroup and the client uses it.
    Core idea belongs to the Visor

    The routing change is a consequence of the RecordingGroup / orchestration model (see ChronoVisor → “Process orchestration & service registry”): a story is bound to a group whose Player is assigned, so there is no pool of Player servers for the client to choose among. It is not a Player decision.

  7. Data access is group-partitioned, not shared-storage global. In the paper the Player is deployed on all storage nodes and reads from shared, distributed storage, and the client picks any Player — so any Player can serve any chronicle. In the implementation a story's data is reachable only through its own recording group's Player: AcquireStory routes the client to that one Player, and the group's Grapher wrote the HDF5 files to its own local directory in the first place. Data is effectively siloed per recording group rather than globally accessible.
    Consequence of one-Player routing + local storage

    This is not a standalone read decision — it falls out of the Visor assigning one Player per group (see “Client routing” above) and the Grapher writing to a local, non-shared directory (see ChronoGrapher → “Storage destination”). The costs are real: a hot story's reads cannot be load-balanced across Players (only one holds the data); that Player is a single point of access — if it or its node is down, the data is unreadable even though it still exists on disk; and there are no cross-group / global reads of a chronicle. The paper's shared-storage, any-Player model avoids all three.

Areas of Research, Analysis & Improvement

Unlike the Grapher, the Player has no standalone Research problem: its gaps are “restore the paper's design,” and the genuinely open questions it touches (clock, durability) are system-wide and covered in other tabs. What follows are the design analyses.

1 · Complete the live-tier read — the cross-tier merge Analysis

The Player already ingests live chunks into PlayerDataStore, but the read path is stubbed (active_window_boundary = 1, get_active_story_events commented; PlaybackService.cpp.new is the work in progress). Finishing the wiring is the easy half. The design-worthy half is the cross-tier merge: serving one consistent read across the live RAM tier and the HDF5 archive while chunks migrate between them. The boundary moves as chunks decay from Player RAM into Grapher-persisted files, so a naive split risks gaps (a chunk in neither tier mid-handoff) or duplicates (a chunk briefly in both) — it needs a watermark / overlap-and-dedup design. Why it matters: this is what closes the freshness gap and delivers the paper's headline read — “read the whole log including the live tail in one call.” (Difference: Reads only the archive.)

2 · Un-silo the data: shared storage + any-Player reads Analysis

Today a story is served only by its group's Player, reading that group's local files, so reads cannot be load-balanced and a Player loss makes its data unreadable though it exists on disk. The decision: restore the paper's shared-storage, any-Player model — a shared / distributed store (parallel FS or object store) plus routing that lets any Player serve any story. To evaluate: the gains (read load-balancing, fault tolerance) against the cost and complexity of shared storage and the loss of data locality. It is the read-side complement of the Grapher's “auto-tiering & distributed destination.” (Differences: Client routing; Data access is group-partitioned.)

3 · Restore the read query optimizers Analysis

Range reads (vs. whole-file over-read), ~4 MB subrequest splitting, range dedup, replay-epoch batching, and constraint pushdown were all dropped. They share one precondition: they only pay off once reads go parallel and multi-tier. So evaluate them as a bundle gated on items 1–2, not piecemeal — adding dedup / epoch batching to a single-Player, single-tier, whole-file reader buys almost nothing, while range reads and constraint pushdown become valuable the moment files grow or reads parallelize. (Differences: Whole-file reads; No constraint filter; Query-optimizer stages dropped.)

Client

Client (Paper version)

A thin but active library that does the time-critical work. It registers with the Visor and fetches the global clock's base value + drift rate, computes a ChronoTick per event without changing its own machine clock, hashes that tick to choose a Keeper, and reads via tail-hashmap playback or a randomly chosen Player.

At a glance

RoleTurns application calls into time-ordered events and routes them
ClockFetches (base, rate) from the Visor; computes its own distance + drift
Write targethash(ChronoTick) → Keeper serverID (uniform; locality-aware optional)
ReadPlayback via the tail hashmap; replay via a randomly chosen Player

Responsibilities

ConnectRegister with the Visor, receive the base clock + drift rate, and measure network latency L (used for the acceptance window).
TimestampPer event compute ChronoTick = current_time / drift_rate + clock_distance.
RecordChoose a Keeper by hashing the ChronoTick, then send a bundled record RPC (data + index + tail update).
Playbackget_tail on the tail-hashmap server → find max ChronoTick → play() that server.
ReplaySend to a randomly chosen Player with a range + constraint.

Note: reflects the client behavior described in the paper (§III.A.3 & III.E).

Client (Implementation)

A C++ chronolog::Client facade over a singleton impl. It registers with the Visor (with a protocol-version handshake), stamps events with its own raw local clock, picks a Keeper by timestamp % n, and reads by sending a time-range query to the single Visor-assigned Player. There is no clock sync, no ChronoTick, and no latency measurement.

Source: client/cpp/ — chronolog_client.h, ChronologClientImpl.cpp, StorytellerClient.cpp, ClientQueryService.cpp, rpcVisorClient.h, PlaybackQueryRpcClient.cpp.

At a glance

LayersClient (public) → ChronologClientImpl (singleton orchestrator) → StorytellerClient (write) + ClientQueryService (read) + RpcVisorClient (control).
ModesWriter-only vs writer + reader (reader mode stands up an inbound query service); ReplayStory is gated to reader mode.
ClientIdPacked (ip<<32 | port<<16 | pid&0xFFFF) — port is the query port for readers, 0 for writers.
ClockNone — raw high_resolution_clock per event.

Write path

AcquireAcquireStory → the Visor returns {StoryId, [Keeper ServiceIds], Player ServiceId}; the client builds a StoryWritingHandle with one KeeperRecordingClient per Keeper.
log_eventStamps eventTime = high_resolution_clock and eventIndex = a per-client atomic counter; chooses Keeper = vectorOfKeepers[eventTime % n] (the class is named RoundRobinKeeperChoice but the behavior is timestamp-modulo); sends one record_event RPC carrying the LogEvent; returns eventTime.

Read path

ReplayReplayStory → ClientQueryService → send_story_playback_request(myServiceId, query_id, chronicle, story, start, end) to the assigned Player. Time range only — no constraint.
ResponseThe Player calls back receive_query_response via RDMA bulk; the client deserializes one PlaybackQueryResponse (a flat vector<Event>) and appends / invokes the callback. dispatch_query polls until done or a 180 s timeout.

Not present absent

Clock / ticksNo clock base/drift fetch, no ChronoTick, no latency L / acceptance window. The ChronologTimer "clockProxy" and the chrono_tick parameter name are vestiges of the intended-but-unbuilt clock sync.

Verified against the files above on develop (deep read of the connect / acquire / write / read paths).

Gaps

The client keeps the paper's shape (connect → acquire → log_event → replay) but is clock-free and explicitly addressed rather than time-hashed. Every clock-dependent behavior fell away with the deferred global clock; routing is handed to it by the Visor instead.

AspectPaper versionImplementation (develop)
Clock syncFetch (base, rate), compute distance + drift. removed None — raw local clock.
Event identityCompute a ChronoTick. reframed Stamp raw timestamp + a per-client atomic index.
Keeper choicehash(ChronoTick) → server; locality-aware optional. changed timestamp % n over the Visor-supplied Keeper set (fixed policy).
Record RPCBundled data + index + tail update. simplified One record_event carrying only the event.
Tail readget_tail → max tick → play(). absent No tail path; time-range replay only.
Player selectionClient randomly picks a Player. changed Visor assigns one Player at acquire.
Replay argsRange vector + constraint. changed One [start, end) time window, no constraint.
Latency LMeasured at connect / acquire. absent Not measured (only a fixed 180 s read timeout).

Why they differ

Deferred clockThe global clock was deferred, so everything depending on it — ChronoTick, hash-to-Keeper, latency / acceptance window — fell away. The client stamps its own time and spreads writes by timestamp-modulo.
Explicit addressingThe Visor's RecordingGroup binding hands the client its exact Keeper set and one Player, so neither hash-routing nor random selection is needed.
Tail folded inTail-read became a recent-window replay (consistent with the API tab), so there is no tail-hashmap consumer on the client.
VestigesChronologTimer, chrono_tick, and RoundRobinKeeperChoice are names that mark where the paper's mechanics were stubbed and then left.

Net effect: a faithful connect → acquire → record → replay lifecycle, but routed by explicit Visor-supplied addresses on a raw local clock — not the self-timing, tick-hashing client the paper describes.

Overview

Scope

Before prioritizing the differences and improvements catalogued across the component tabs, we need to name the end goal. ChronoLog could become several different things, and the same analysis re-reads differently depending on which we target. Three broad scenarios — to be reframed and specified as we work:

1 · Research project — validate the thesis

Not a product. Forget usability, deployment, users, and breadth of functionality. The goal is to prove or test the original paper's thesis with just enough of a system to measure. Candidate questions: does physical time as the ordering primitive actually remove the sequencer bottleneck and scale? Does multi-tier auto-tiering deliver the capacity and tail/historical I/O isolation it claims? Does MWMR / parallel I/O beat single-writer systems by the margin claimed? And the genuinely open one we surfaced: can you have durability and throughput at once? The deliverable is evidence — benchmarks, clock-uncertainty modeling, demos — not a system people run.

2 · Data-center product — realize the full vision

A real, deployable log system for HPC, clusters, and data centers. Here the differences we catalogued become the roadmap: every gap is a to-do — durability and high availability, MWMR parallel writes (PHDF5), auto-tiering across distributed storage, elasticity, a real deployment layer, and authorization. This is the most work and the largest distance from today's code — it means closing, rather than living with, the implementation's simplifications.

3 · ChronoLog-lite — a local, embeddable time-ordered log

Drop the cluster requirement; keep the time-ordering value. Something easier and available to more people — no whole cluster needed to run it. Concretely it could be a single-node or embeddable time-ordered log (a “SQLite for time-logs”), an edge / IoT logger, or a local time-series store: single binary, no RecordingGroups, no distributed storage. It trades the paper's scale ambitions for reach.

Why this tab is the lens. The same differences read in opposite directions depending on the target. For the data-center product (2), the implementation's simplifications — local storage, single-process, mutex-guarded, one-Player-per-group — are gaps to close. For ChronoLog-lite (3), those same simplifications are assets and a head start: the code has already drifted toward “smaller,” away from the distributed vision. The research project (1) cares about neither — it just needs enough to measure. So #3 is arguably closest to today's reality, #2 the furthest, and picking one re-prioritizes every research / improvement item in the other tabs.

Where the real users are — three concrete directions

Working the scenarios, the value question kept converging on one statement: ChronoLog's edge is real only where someone needs correct, high-volume, time-ordered event streaming in an environment existing tools fit badly. Testing the alternatives against incumbents narrows the field fast: a generic local store loses to SQLite / DuckDB / RocksDB; agent memory is a semantic-relevance problem owned by vector DBs; agent observability is owned by Langfuse / LangSmith; the general data-center log is owned by Kafka. What survives is the environment Kafka genuinely cannot serve — HPC and scientific facilities — plus one cheap consumer-side probe. Direction A is the at-scale form of scenario 2, Direction B is the wedge into it, and Direction C is what remains of scenario 3 / the “AgentLog” idea.

Direction A — at scale: the event backbone for HPC facilities

HPC centers increasingly need streaming — telemetry, job events, coupling simulations to live analysis — and Kafka does not fit on a supercomputer: batch allocations instead of long-running services, RDMA fabrics it cannot use, parallel filesystems instead of local disks, no root. Today centers cobble together LDMS (metrics), Darshan (I/O logs), flat files, and grafted-on InfluxDB / Prometheus. There is no native ordered-event substrate for a supercomputer. The users are the operations, telemetry, and workflow teams at DOE / NSF facilities — Argonne, ORNL, LLNL, NERSC, TACC, NCSA — and their European counterparts (JSC, CSC, BSC).

Concrete use cases

  1. Full-machine telemetry. Job events, node health, and I/O statistics at millions of events per second across thousands of nodes — the one workload where the sequencer-free ordering thesis actually matters. Today fragmented across LDMS, Darshan, and ad-hoc files.
  2. AI-coupled workflows. Simulations streaming training data to models and receiving steering signals back — the fastest-growing HPC pattern, with no native event plumbing.
  3. In-situ / in-transit analysis coupling. Staging simulation events to live analysis pipelines without first writing everything to the parallel filesystem.
  4. Workflow provenance. A totally-ordered, time-replayable record of what a distributed scientific campaign did — auditable and reproducible.
The gap we fill

A time-indexed, totally-ordered event store that is native to the HPC environment: Mochi / Thallium stack, RDMA transports, batch-friendly deployment, storage tiered along the time axis. Every current alternative is either fragmented (LDMS + Darshan + files) or a cloud tool fighting the environment (Kafka, InfluxDB). Honest sizing: dozens of facilities, not a mass market — this is infrastructure adoption on the Darshan / ADIOS2 path, which is exactly what an NSF-funded system is positioned for.

Direction B — the wedge: scientific-instrument & experiment data streaming

The sharpest concrete target. Light sources (APS, NSLS-II, LCLS), electron microscopes, fusion diagnostics, and telescopes emit high-rate, inherently time-ordered event streams that must be buffered hot for prompt analysis while the experiment runs, archived durably, and replayed by time window for reanalysis. That is, item for item, ChronoLog's data model: tail tier + archive tier + time-range replay. The users are nameable: beamline software groups (the Bluesky ecosystem at NSLS-II / APS), LCLS data systems, fusion diagnostics teams.

Concrete use cases

  1. Prompt analysis during a run. Tail-read detector events seconds after acquisition to steer the experiment while beam time is burning.
  2. Time-window reanalysis. “All detector events between T1 and T2 of run 47” — ChronoLog's native query, served from the archive with no auxiliary index.
  3. Cross-stream correlation. Beam state + sample environment + detector streams correlated by time — the primary index — rather than joined after the fact.
  4. Instrument → compute-facility streaming. The DOE Integrated Research Infrastructure (IRI) pattern — streaming experiment data to HPC for live processing — which is being funded now, and which the APS upgrade (~100× more data) makes urgent.
The gap we fill

The missing queryable time-store between instrument and analysis. ADIOS2 moves data but is not a store you can query; Kafka stores but cannot time-range query and fits the facility environment badly; Bluesky's event model needs a backend (today MongoDB / Kafka). ChronoLog slots in as the store and integrates with, rather than fights, that stack. Crucially, what the component tabs treated as compromises are assets here: the HDF5 archive is the lingua franca of facility science, and per-group locality matches per-instrument deployment. Sizing: tens of facilities, hundreds of beamlines, funded engineers — a niche with an acute, currently-funded pain and no purpose-built incumbent.

Direction C — agile probe: the agent flight recorder

The most defensible consumer-side option — framed precisely. Not agent memory (vector DBs own semantic relevance) and not agent observability dashboards (Langfuse / LangSmith own that). The unowned sliver is deterministic record-and-replay: a black-box flight recorder that captures every event of an agent system in order and can re-run a session exactly — time-travel debugging for agents, shipped as a small pip-installable OSS library.

Concrete use cases

  1. Replay a failed session exactly. Multi-agent failures are “worked in isolation, broke together” — replay the true interleaving instead of guessing from scattered logs.
  2. Regression-test agents against recorded histories. Re-run yesterday's sessions against today's prompt or model change and diff the behavior.
  3. Audit trail. An ordered, immutable record of what the agent decided and when, for compliance-sensitive deployments.
The gap we fill

Incumbents store traces to look at; nobody owns replay semantics. Agent debugging is a felt, daily pain, and a recorder with first-class time-ordered replay is a tool people would adopt quickly.

Why this is a probe, not a bet

It uses almost none of ChronoLog's actual novelty — single-node-ish, low event rates, effectively a “lite” re-skin. The space is funded and fast-moving: an incumbent could add replay in a quarter. And the runner-up in this category — a robotics data recorder, technically a beautiful fit (sensor fusion, rosbag-style replay, onboard→offload tiering) — faces a strong, beloved incumbent in MCAP / Foxglove. So Direction C is a cheap experiment for learning and visibility, not a direction to bet the architecture on.

Reading the three together

DirectionUsersPain today?Uses the novelty?Incumbent riskFit to code & grant
A · HPC backboneFacility ops / workflow teamsYes FullyNone nativeHigh
B · Instrument streamingBeamline / experiment software groups Acute & funded (IRI)MostlyPartial (ADIOS2 / Kafka, both incomplete) Highest
C · Agent flight recorderAI engineersYes (debugging) BarelyHigh, fast-movingLow

The realistic future users wear facility badges, not startup hoodies. Direction B is the wedge — concrete, funded, nameable users, and the codebase's “compromises” (HDF5 archive, chunked files, group locality) are strengths there. Direction A is what B grows into. Direction C is worth at most a cheap OSS experiment for learning and visibility — it is not where this architecture wins. The sequence that follows: prove the thesis (scenario 1) on Direction B workloads, then harden into A.
